Reference
The Depot

Before you startSystem Design: The Depot#

A very short book for engineers who are asked, in every design review, what happens under load, where the data lives and which copy is right.

The promise

Read this in three evenings and you will be able to take a feature with a stated load and a stated volume of data, estimate it on one sheet of paper, choose how to store, copy, split and cache its data, say what consistency each operation needs, protect it from overload and from the loss of a region, and defend each choice against anyone who says "web scale" with confidence.

It reads as one story. Bramble is an online stationery shop whose system is well organised and has never been busy. Then its founder books a television feature, a back-to-school sale, a launch on a second continent and a limited-edition drop with half a million people arriving at 09:00. Every chapter starts with something breaking. The fix is the chapter's idea. By the end of the chapter, the fix has opened a new crack.

Most ideas arrive four ways: a place in one running metaphor (a network of depots holding stock and serving lorries), a diagram of the mechanism, a one-sentence Remember it as line you can say out loud, and a dated account of who thought of it, when, and what they were reacting to. Every chapter then does what a mentor would do at a whiteboard: it names the traps and their tell-tale signs, gives you a small design with one planted flaw to find, and hands you three questions to ask whoever proposes the mechanism next, plus the one point on which respected practitioners still disagree, argued fairly from both sides.

Who this is for

You build or review systems that other people depend on. You have heard "replica", "shard", "quorum", "CAP" and "p99" in meetings and nodded. You want the part of the field that lets you lead a design review, without reading six hundred pages on each topic first.

The level is "can lead the design review", not "can implement the database". If you have run a sharded datastore in production, been paged for a split brain and can state the CAP theorem as it was proved, this book will be too slow for you; skim the At the whiteboard boxes, chapter 20 and the epilogue.

How to read it

  • Straight through the first time. The plot carries the ideas.
  • The numbers are fixed. Bramble has one set of figures (orders a day, requests a second, rows, bytes), and every calculation in the book uses them. When a chapter says "not yet", it says at what number the answer changes.
  • The Epilogue is the reference: the metaphor table, the review checklist, a numbers card, the design method on one card, the timeline of the field and a reading list by year.

The cast, and where Bramble stands

Bramble sells stationery online: its own range, other sellers' goods, and a monthly subscription box. Its system is split along the lines of the business into a handful of services (Catalogue, which shows products; Ordering, which takes orders; Billing; Fulfilment, which owns stock and ships; Promotions), each with its own database on its own single machine, and they tell one another what happened by sending messages through a broker. Ana is its architect: good at deciding what belongs in which service, and a beginner at everything in this book. Kofi is the staff engineer who has been paged for most of these failures before and carries the history. Priya leads Catalogue and proposes the first fix, which is the natural one and usually wrong in a way worth watching. Marcus is the consultant who proposes what the largest companies run; his arguments are the real ones, and when he is wrong it is because Bramble's numbers do not meet his premise, not because he is foolish. Lena founded the company and keeps selling more than the system can serve.

Code, where it appears, is Java 21 and SQL from Bramble's stock and order tables.

The sibling books

This is the second of three. DDD and Microservices: The Atlas tells how Bramble found its boundaries and owns everything about where they go and how the parts talk: bounded contexts, aggregates, idempotency keys, the outbox, sagas and contract tests. When this book needs one of those it names the Atlas chapter in a sentence and moves on. This book owns data, scale and reliability. A third, on software architecture, owns system-level styles, the analysis of trade-offs and decision records.

Dates and sources

Every "who and when" was checked against the source named in research/milestones.md in the book's repository, which says where only a secondary source could be found, and the theorems of chapters 13 to 15 are stated as their papers state them, with the quotations recorded in the same file. There are no hardware prices and no product limits, because those date within a year.

Chapter 1 · Act IThe Morning the Shop Went Viral#

The problem

At 07:42 on a Tuesday a breakfast-television presenter holds up Bramble's weekly planner and says she has bought one for everyone she knows. Lena booked the feature three weeks ago and mentioned it to engineering on Monday.

Ana is watching the dashboard when it happens. Product-page traffic, which peaks at 150 views a second on a busy evening, passes 1,500. The tile she trusts, average response time, moves from 90 milliseconds to 190. Amber starts at 500. It looks like a system working a little harder.

It is not. Support's inbox fills with screenshots of a blank page. Lena, at home, cannot load her own shop. Priya has the fix ready: Catalogue's app server is at 100% CPU, so add servers. It would take a day; nothing at Bramble has ever run as more than one copy.

Kofi asks a different question first: where was that average measured? On the server, from the moment a request starts being handled to the moment it finishes. He opens the log of the web proxy that sits in front of it, which stamps each request when it arrives. Half the customers waited more than 2 seconds. One in a hundred waited 14. A great many gave up, and a request that is abandoned in the queue is never timed at all.

The server was timing the work. The customers were timing the wait.

The idea

Think of the shop as a depot. A request is a lorry arriving at the gate and leaving loaded. Two numbers describe how the depot is doing, and they are not the same number.

Latency Throughput
The question How long did one lorry wait, gate to gate? How many lorries left this hour?
Unit Milliseconds per request Requests per second
Who feels it The customer The capacity plan
How to report it As percentiles, measured where the customer is As a rate, with the peak beside the average

Latency is a distribution, and an average flattens it. Report percentiles: p50 is the time half the requests beat; p95 and p99 are the times that 95 and 99 in a hundred beat. On an ordinary evening Bramble's product page has a p50 of 90 ms and a p99 of 1.9 seconds, and nobody knew, because the average said 120. That slow end is tail latency: the slowest lorry in a hundred, which is the one that complains. A customer who views twenty pages has an 18% chance of meeting the p99 at least once (1 − 0.99²⁰), and the customers who load most pages are the ones who buy most.

Why did the tail explode? Utilisation is how full the loading bays are: the share of time a resource is busy. Saturation is the queue down the road when they are all full: work that has arrived and cannot start. Lorries do not arrive evenly, so a queue forms well before the bays are full on average, and the wait grows out of all proportion to the load. For one server whose work takes 20 ms:

Utilisation Typical response time Compared with idle
50% 40 ms 2 ×
80% 100 ms 5 ×
90% 200 ms 10 ×
95% 400 ms 20 ×
99% 2,000 ms 100 ×

The rule behind the table is response = service time ÷ (1 − utilisation). Between 50% and 80% nothing seems to happen. Between 90% and 99% the wait grows tenfold for a tenth more traffic. Past 100% there is no steady state at all: the queue grows until something drops lorries.

The diagram also shows the bottleneck: the one narrow gate every lorry must pass. That morning it was the app server's processors, which can render 285 pages a second and no more. The database behind it was 20% busy. Making the database faster would have changed nothing; adding capacity anywhere but the bottleneck never does.

The first money to spend is usually on scaling up: a bigger depot. Kofi resizes the server from 8 cores to 32. It takes eleven minutes and no code. The rest of the day runs at 450 views a second and the bigger machine takes it at under half busy. Scale up first because it is fast, it changes nothing in the software, and one machine has no copies to keep in step. The rule has three limits. A single machine is a single point of failure, however large. The price curve bends: the largest machines cost far more per core than the mid-sized ones. And the gain is less than the cores. Amdahl's law says that if a fraction of the work cannot be shared out, that fraction caps the speed-up: with 5% of the work serial on today's server, four times the cores gives 3.5 times the throughput, and no number of cores gives more than twenty. Bramble's 32 cores saturate near 1,000 views a second, not 1,140. Scaling out, the alternative, has no such ceiling, but it costs a load balancer, shared state and a deployment that must work in more than one place.

Remember it as: time the wait, not the work; watch the slowest lorry in a hundred; a depot nine-tenths full already has a queue down the road.

◷How we got hereAgner Krarup Erlang, an engineer at the Copenhagen Telephone Company, published the founding paper of…

Agner Krarup Erlang, an engineer at the Copenhagen Telephone Company, published the founding paper of queueing theory in 1909, showing that telephone calls arrive in a random pattern that can be calculated, and by 1917 had formulae for a commercial question: how many lines does an exchange need so that callers rarely find them all busy? Gene Amdahl, defending the single large processor against parallel machines in 1967, gave the limit on what adding processors can buy. The modern concern with the tail comes from Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso, whose 2013 article "The Tail at Scale" observed that when one page fans out to a hundred servers, the rare slow response becomes the common experience, and that averages were hiding it. Each was reacting to the same mistake: sizing a system for its typical moment.

⚠The traps
  • Averages that hide the tail: the sign is a dashboard whose only latency tile is a mean, measured on the server. The slowest requests, and every request that gave up while queueing, are invisible until customers report them.
  • Scaling out before measuring: the sign is a proposal to add servers that does not name the saturated resource. If the bottleneck is elsewhere, the new servers idle and the queue stays.
  • Running hot: the sign is a resource at 85% or more on a normal peak, described as efficient. There is no room for a burst, and the queueing table says latency is already five to ten times the idle figure.
  • Coordinated omission: the sign is a load test whose generator waits for each reply before sending the next request. When the server stalls the generator stalls with it, so the slow period is barely sampled and the reported percentiles are far too good.
◉Spot it

A load-test report for the new product page: "Fifty virtual users. Each sends a request, waits for the reply, then sends the next. Sustained 600 requests a second for ten minutes. p50 78 ms, p99 140 ms, measured at the load generator. The server paused twice for about four seconds during garbage collection; the percentiles were not affected. Conclusion: the page meets its p99 target of 200 ms."

Show the answer

Answer The generator waits for each reply before sending again, so during each four-second pause it sent fifty requests instead of the 2,400 that real customers would have sent. The sign is the sentence "the percentiles were not affected" beside an eight-second stall: that is coordinated omission. The fix is a generator that sends at a fixed rate regardless of replies and times each request from the moment it was due, not the moment it was sent.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What is the p99 latency at peak, measured where the customer is, and what was it last week?
  2. Which resource saturates first as load rises, and at how many requests per second?
  3. How busy is that resource at today's normal peak, as a percentage?

Still argued: how far to scale up before scaling out. Nick Craver's account of Stack Overflow's architecture (2016) describes one of the busiest sites on the web served by a small number of large machines: eleven web servers and four database servers. The case for such a design is that big hardware is cheap next to engineers and that a system with few moving parts fails in fewer ways. Luiz André Barroso and Urs Hölzle, in The Datacenter as a Computer (2009), argue the opposite from Google's experience: many modest machines cost less per unit of work. Since any machine will fail, the software must tolerate failure anyway, so it may as well be built for many from the start. Both agree that a single machine cannot be the final answer for a service that must stay up. They differ on how long the simple design should be kept, and the honest answer depends on a number: how close the largest affordable machine is to your peak.

What Ana learned

  • Measure latency as p50, p95 and p99 at the customer's side of the queue, and put those on the dashboard instead of the mean.
  • Find the resource that saturates first before spending anything, and keep it under about 70% busy at peak.
  • Reach for a bigger machine first, and write down the two things it does not fix: the ceiling and the single point of failure.

…but

The bigger machine holds. Then Lena announces the back-to-school sale: ten times a normal day, in August. Priya says to resize the machine again. Nobody in the room can say whether that is too little, too much, or whether such a machine exists.

Chapter 2 · Act IThe Back of the Envelope#

The problem

Lena wants one answer by Friday: will the shop hold on sale day? She gets three. Priya says to resize the machine again, because resizing worked last time. The hosting account manager says Bramble should take the largest machine on the price list, to be safe. Finance says the budget line for August is whatever engineering can justify, and so far nobody has justified anything.

Ana notices that none of the three answers contains a number of requests. "Ten times a normal day" is the only figure anyone has, and it is a statement about a day. Machines do not fall over across a day. They fall over in the worst minute of it.

Priya has run a test, to be fair. She pointed a script at the product page and measured 3,000 views a second on the original server, which would make the television morning impossible to explain. Kofi reads the script. It requests one product, the weekly planner, as one customer, over and over. After the first request everything it needs is in memory. The real catalogue has 200,000 products and most requests are for something the server has not looked at recently.

Kofi takes a sheet of paper and says the meeting will not end until the sheet has a number for the worst minute, and a second number for what one machine can do about it.

The idea

Back-of-the-envelope estimation is arithmetic with round numbers, done before any design, to find out which of your problems are real. It has four moves.

From a day to a second. A day has 86,400 seconds. Call it 100,000: the sum becomes a matter of dropping five zeros, and the answer is 14% low, which will not matter. Bramble serves 5,000,000 product pages on a normal day, so about 50 requests per second on average; 50,000 orders is one every two seconds.

From average to peak. Traffic is not flat. Bramble's weekday evening runs at three times the daily average: 150 views a second. A sale is burstier, because an email lands in two million inboxes at 09:00, so Kofi uses a factor of four on a day that is itself ten times normal.

From requests to resources. Each product page costs five database queries and weighs 1 MB, of which 50 KB is the page Bramble computes and the rest is images, styles and scripts. Each order stores about 1 KB plus three lines of 0.25 KB.

Sale day Arithmetic Estimate
Page views, average 50,000,000 ÷ 100,000 s 500 per second
Page views, peak × 4 2,000 per second
Orders, peak 500,000 ÷ 100,000 s × 4 20 per second
Database queries, peak 2,000 × 5 10,000 per second
Bandwidth, peak 2,000 × 1 MB 2 GB per second, which is 16 Gbit per second
Storage for the day's orders 500,000 × 1.75 KB under 1 GB

Two rows are worth the whole exercise. Storage is nothing: a year of orders is about 32 GB, so no decision should be driven by disk. Bandwidth is alarming: 16 Gbit a second is more than Bramble's connection carries. Kofi circles it and writes "later" beside it.

From resources to machines. This needs one measured figure, and a few orders of magnitude to judge designs by before anything is measured:

Operation Time If a memory read took one second
Read from memory 100 ns 1 second
Read from a solid-state disk 100 µs 17 minutes
Round trip inside one data centre 0.5 ms 83 minutes
Round trip between continents 150 ms 17 days

Memory is a thousand times faster than disk and a million times faster than another continent. Most of this book is a consequence of that table.

The measured figure comes from testing, and there are three kinds. A load test applies the expected peak with a realistic mix and asks whether latency holds. A stress test keeps raising the rate until something breaks, to learn what breaks first and how. A soak test holds a realistic load for hours, to find what leaks. Priya reruns hers with the real catalogue and a production-shaped mix. One 8-core server saturates near 285 views a second.

Nobody should plan to run at saturation; chapter 1's table says why. Headroom is the gap you leave on purpose: plan for the bottleneck to be about 70% busy at the estimated peak, which leaves room for the estimate to be wrong and for a burst inside the peak. At 70%, one server is good for 200 views a second, so the sale needs 2,000 ÷ 200 = 10 servers' worth, and 12 with two spare. The rule bends for work nobody is waiting for: a batch job may run a machine at 95%, because a queue of jobs is not a queue of customers. The cost of headroom is paying for capacity that is idle most of the year, and chapter 19 sends the bill.

The largest machine on the price list has 96 cores, twelve times the original. Amdahl's law with 5% serial work turns twelve times the cores into 7.7 times the throughput: about 2,200 views a second at saturation and 1,540 at 70%. It is short of 2,000, and it is one machine.

Capacity planning is this page kept up to date: the forecast, the measured capacity, and the date on which one crosses the other.

Remember it as: drop five zeros to get from a day to a second, multiply for the peak, and leave a third of every machine empty.

◷How we got herePhysicists call these Fermi estimates, after Enrico Fermi, who in 1945 judged the yield of the first atomic…

Physicists call these Fermi estimates, after Enrico Fermi, who in 1945 judged the yield of the first atomic test by dropping scraps of paper as the blast wave passed. Jon Bentley brought the habit to programmers in his "Programming Pearls" columns, collected as a book in 1986, where "the back of the envelope" has a chapter of its own. Jeff Dean gave engineers the numbers to do it with: a slide of "numbers everyone should know" in talks about building Google's systems, widely circulated from his 2009 keynote, listing what a memory reference, a disk seek and a packet to another continent each cost. The hardware has changed since and the ratios mostly have not. Each of them was reacting to engineers who designed first and discovered the quantities afterwards.

⚠The traps
  • Designing for the average day: the sign is a capacity figure obtained by dividing a daily total by the seconds in a day and stopping there. The system is sized for a load it only sees at four in the morning.
  • False precision: the sign is an estimate of 57.87 requests per second built on a peak factor somebody guessed. The digits invite trust the inputs have not earned; round to one figure and state the assumption.
  • Load testing with unrealistic data: the sign is a test that requests one product, as one user, against an empty database. Everything is served from memory and the result is several times too good.
  • No headroom: the sign is a plan in which estimated peak equals measured capacity. Any error in the estimate, or one machine lost, is an outage.
◉Spot it

A capacity note for sale day: "Fifty million page views are expected. A day is about 100,000 seconds, so that is 500 views a second. Our load test, run with the full catalogue and a production mix, shows one server is good for 200 views a second at 70% busy. Three servers cover 500 with room over; we will run four so that one can fail. Storage is not a concern at under 1 GB for the day."

Show the answer

Answer The note sizes for the daily average and never multiplies for the peak. The sign is that the only division is by the length of the day. At four times the average the worst hour brings 2,000 views a second, which needs ten servers at 70% and twelve with spares; four servers would be saturated by mid-morning. Everything else in the note is sound.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What is the peak rate in requests per second, and what multiple of the daily average is it?
  2. At that peak, how busy is the bottleneck, and how much headroom is left?
  3. Was the load test run with production-sized data and a production-shaped mix of requests?

Still argued: how much to trust arithmetic before the system exists. Jon Bentley (1986) holds that a few minutes of estimation should precede any design, because it removes whole classes of solution before anyone builds them. Being wrong by a factor of two, he adds, still tells you which problems are real. John Allspaw, in The Art of Capacity Planning (2008), holds that capacity is found by measuring the production system under its real workload, because benchmarks and models miss the interactions that set the true ceiling. Forecasts, on his account, should be drawn from observed history. The two are less opposed than they sound, since Bentley estimates in order to decide what to measure and Allspaw measures in order to correct the estimate. The disagreement that remains is about which to believe when they differ, and a new system has no history to consult.

What Ana learned

  • Put a peak rate in requests per second on the first page of every design, with the multiplier and where it came from.
  • Size the bottleneck for 70% busy at that peak, and state what the spare third is for.
  • Believe a load test only after reading what data and what mix of requests it used.

…but

The sheet says the sale needs ten servers' worth of work and that no single machine, at any price, supplies it. On Sunday the one machine Bramble has is restarted for a security patch, and the shop is closed for eleven minutes.

Chapter 3 · Act ITwo of Everything#

The problem

The sheet from chapter 2 says the sale needs ten servers' worth of work, and Sunday's eleven-minute restart says one machine is one failure. So on Monday Priya does the obvious thing: a second Catalogue server, and a load balancer in front of the pair.

By Tuesday support has a new kind of ticket. Baskets empty themselves. Customers are signed out halfway through checkout. A seller uploads a spreadsheet of new prices, and on every second refresh the import page says no file was received. Ana works it out at the whiteboard: the basket and the sign-in live in the memory of whichever server handled the request, the spreadsheet was written to that server's disk, and the load balancer sends the next request to the other one.

Priya's fix takes one line of configuration: sticky sessions, so that each customer always returns to the same server. The tickets stop. On Wednesday a routine deploy restarts server two, and every customer who was stuck to it loses their basket at once. On Thursday the television planner is featured again in a newspaper, one server gets most of the returning customers, and it runs at 95% while its neighbour idles.

Kofi's summary: Bramble now has two machines and has gained neither capacity nor safety, because each customer still depends on exactly one of them.

The idea

There are two ways to get more work done, and they fail differently.

Scaling up Scaling out
What it is A bigger depot More depots
Ceiling The largest machine sold None in principle
When one machine fails Everything stops One share of capacity is lost
What it costs A steeper price per core A load balancer, shared state, many deploys

Scaling out only works if the servers are interchangeable. A stateless service is a bay where any loader can serve any lorry, because nothing is kept at the bay. Everything a request needs arrives with it or is fetched from somewhere shared. For Bramble that means two moves. Session state, the basket and the sign-in, goes into a store all servers can reach, keyed by the session cookie. Uploaded files go to shared storage. After that, any server can answer any request, a restart loses nothing, and sticky sessions can be switched off.

The load balancer is the dispatcher at the gate, and there are two kinds. A layer 4 balancer forwards network connections: it sees addresses and ports, is very fast, and knows nothing of what is inside. A layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request: it can send /checkout to one pool and images to another, retry a failed request elsewhere, and terminate encryption. Bramble needs the second. How the dispatcher chooses a bay matters less than people expect, with one exception:

  • Round robin: each server in turn. Fair when requests cost about the same.
  • Least connections: the server with the fewest requests in flight. Better when costs vary, but every dispatcher acting on the same slightly stale counts sends a herd to the same server.
  • Power of two choices: pick two servers at random and use the less busy. Nearly as even as least connections, with no herd.

The dispatcher must also know which bays are staffed. A health check is its glance: a request every few seconds to an endpoint on each server, and a server that fails is taken out of rotation. What the endpoint tests is a design decision. Too shallow, a static "OK", and a server whose database connections are all dead keeps receiving customers. Too deep, a query against the database, and one database hiccup marks every server unhealthy at once and takes the whole shop down. Test what this server alone can break.

Now count what is left that exists only once. A single point of failure is the only bridge into the estate, and redundancy is building a second one. It counts only if the two fail independently, so the copies go in different zones: separate buildings with separate power and network. Two load balancers, one per zone. Twelve servers, six per zone, so that the sale's ten survive the loss of two.

Every topology in this book is drawn this way. A solid arrow is a request that waits for its answer. A dashed arrow is a transfer nobody waits for: a queued message, a copy, a cache being filled. A box around nodes is a failure domain, labelled with its kind, and everything inside it can fail together. A green cylinder is a store that takes writes; a copy of one is a paler green. Read the diagram for what stands alone: the session store and the database each exist once, in Zone A.

Redundancy is what buys availability, usually quoted in nines:

Availability Downtime allowed in a year
99% 3.7 days
99.9% 8.8 hours
99.99% 53 minutes
99.999% 5 minutes

Parts in a chain multiply: two 99.9% parts that both must work give 99.8%. Parts in parallel multiply their failures: two independent 99% servers, either of which will do, give 99.99%.

Autoscaling adds and removes servers automatically as a signal crosses a threshold. It pays for itself on daily cycles. It does not catch a spike: a new server takes minutes to start, and a sale email lands in one. For a known event, raise the floor beforehand.

Remember it as: keep nothing at the bay, staff two of everything in different buildings, and let the dispatcher send any lorry anywhere.

◷How we got hereIn the 1990s a busy site scaled by buying a bigger server, and the usual server handled each connection with…

In the 1990s a busy site scaled by buying a bigger server, and the usual server handled each connection with its own process or thread. Dan Kegel's 1999 web page "The C10K problem" argued that it was time one machine served ten thousand clients at once, and catalogued the operating-system techniques that would let it. The event-driven servers that followed made a cheap machine capable of holding tens of thousands of connections, which is what made the software load balancer practical. How it should choose a server has a surprising answer. Yossi Azar and colleagues proved in 1994 that sampling two servers at random and taking the less loaded beats one random choice dramatically, and Michael Mitzenmacher's 2001 paper, which named the idea "the power of two choices", showed that it holds for queues with arrivals and departures. It explains why a balancer need neither choose blindly nor stampede towards whichever server last looked idle.

⚠The traps
  • Sticky sessions as state: the sign is a balancer configured to pin each customer to one server so that their session survives. A restart loses every session on that server, and load cannot be spread evenly.
  • The health check that lies: the sign is a health endpoint that returns a constant, or one that tests a dependency every server shares. The first keeps a broken server in rotation; the second removes every server together.
  • The single load balancer: the sign is a diagram with two of every server and one box in front of them. The redundancy behind it is unreachable when it fails.
  • Autoscaling on the wrong signal: the sign is a scaling rule on a metric the bottleneck does not move, such as memory on a service limited by CPU. The fleet stays small while the queue grows, or grows while the database is the limit.
  • State on local disk: the sign is an upload, a report or a session written to the server's own filesystem. It is visible from one server and gone when that server is replaced.
◉Spot it

Bramble's first two-zone layout for the Ordering service. The app servers are stateless and the stores are not shown.

Show the answer

Answer Both load balancers are in Zone A. The sign is a failure-domain box that contains every copy of one component: the pair fails together when the zone does, and the healthy servers in Zone B cannot be reached. The fix is one balancer per zone.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which single machine, if switched off now, would customers notice?
  2. Where is session state kept, and can any server answer any customer's next request?
  3. What does the health check test, and what happens to the fleet when the thing it tests fails?

Still argued: whether services should be stateless at all. Adam Wiggins's "Twelve-Factor App" (2011) holds that processes must share nothing and keep no session in memory or on disk, because only then can any process be started, stopped or replaced freely. It calls sticky sessions a violation. Caitie McCaffrey's talk "Building Scalable Stateful Services" (2015) holds that keeping a user's data in the memory of the server that handles them gives lower latency and stronger consistency than a round trip to a shared store. Cluster membership and consistent routing make it safe, she argues, citing systems that run this way in production. The first pays a network hop on every request; the second pays in machinery for routing and for moving state when a server dies. For a shop whose pages are mostly reads the field's default is stateless; for games, chat and collaboration it is open.

What Ana learned

  • Move every piece of per-customer state out of the app servers before adding the second one.
  • For each box on the diagram, ask what happens when it is switched off, and put the copies in different zones.
  • Raise capacity ahead of a known event by hand, and leave autoscaling for the daily cycle.

…but

Twelve stateless servers pass the load test at under a quarter busy. The test stops at 800 views a second all the same, because one of the databases behind them is at 100%, and nearly all of that is a single query.

Chapter 4 · Act IIThe Query That Read Every Row#

The problem

The load test stopped at 800 views a second with twelve app servers idling and one database at 100%. The database is Ordering's, and the query log shows where the time goes: the "My orders" page, about one request in a hundred.

On a normal evening that is one or two a second, each taking four seconds, and the database has looked "about 40% busy" for a year without anyone asking why. At 800 views a second it is eight a second. Eight queries arriving each second and each living for four seconds is thirty-two running at once on sixteen cores. They queue. Each holds a database connection while it waits, the app servers run out of connections, and now the cheap queries, the ones behind checkout, cannot get a connection either. One slow page has closed the shop.

Priya's first fix is the one from chapter 3: more app servers. Kofi points out that each new server opens twenty more connections to a database that is already drowning. Her second fix is an index on every column of the orders table, "so it can't happen again".

Ana asks the question she would have asked about a boundary: what, exactly, is the database being asked to do? Kofi types one word in front of the query: EXPLAIN.

The idea

A database answers a query by following a query plan, and it will show you the plan if asked. This one says the database is reading all 40,000,000 orders to find one customer's twenty. That is a full table scan: walking every aisle to find one box.

An index is the aisle signs and the catalogue at the front desk: a second, smaller structure, kept sorted, that says where the rows are. The usual kind is a B-tree: a tree of pages, each holding a few hundred sorted keys and pointers to the pages below. Forty million rows need about four levels, so finding a customer's orders means reading four pages instead of the table.

The index has to match the query. A composite index covers several columns, and their order decides what it is good for: it is sorted by the first column, then by the second within the first. Put the column tested for equality first and the column sorted or ranged on next. An index on (placed_at, customer_id) is sorted by date across all customers and is useless here. A covering index goes one step further and carries every column the query returns, so the table is never visited. In PostgreSQL:

SELECT id, status, total_minor, placed_at
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = 48213
 ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20;

-- Plan before (EXPLAIN ANALYZE, abridged):
--   Sort (top 20)
--     ->  Seq Scan on orders            rows read: 40,000,000
--   Execution time: 4,100 ms

CREATE INDEX orders_by_customer
    ON orders (customer_id, placed_at DESC, id DESC)
    INCLUDE (status, total_minor);

-- Plan after:
--   Index Only Scan using orders_by_customer   rows read: 20
--   Execution time: 0.2 ms

So why not Priya's index on every column? Because every insert and every update must also update every index on the table, and each index competes for memory. Index for the queries you have, found in the slow-query log, and delete the indexes no plan uses. The rule relaxes on a copy that is only read, such as a reporting database, where extra indexes cost disk and little else.

Three more ways one page hurts a database, all on the same screen.

Pagination. "My orders" has a page 2. OFFSET makes the database produce and discard every earlier row, so page 1,000 costs a thousand times page 1. Keyset pagination asks for "the twenty after the last one I showed you", which the index answers directly at any depth. The cost is that you can only move to the next page, not jump to page 400; for an endless list that is no loss.

-- Offset: reads 20,020 rows to return 20
SELECT id, status, total_minor, placed_at
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = 48213
 ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000;

-- Keyset: reads 20 rows, however deep
SELECT id, status, total_minor, placed_at
  FROM orders
 WHERE customer_id = 48213
   AND (placed_at, id) < ('2026-03-14 09:26:53', 39118204)
 ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
 LIMIT 20;

N+1 queries. The page fetches twenty orders, then loops and fetches each order's lines: one query plus twenty. Each is fast and each is a round trip of half a millisecond or more. Fetch the lines for all twenty in one query.

The connection pool. A database connection is expensive to open and costs the database memory while open, so each app server keeps a fixed set: the fixed number of trolleys; a loader without one waits. Twelve servers with twenty each is 240 connections, and the database has a limit. A pool turns slow queries into a visible queue, which is good, provided waiting for a connection has a timeout and the total across all servers is counted.

Underneath, two things are worth knowing by name. The write-ahead log is the goods-in book, written before anything is put on a shelf: every change is appended to a sequential file and flushed to disk before the database says "committed", and the table pages are updated later. After a crash the log is replayed. Chapter 5 copies that log to other machines. And B-trees are not the only engine. An LSM-tree never updates in place: it collects writes in memory, flushes them as sorted files and merges those in the background.

B-tree LSM-tree
Write Finds the page and changes it Appends; merges later
Read One path down the tree May check several files
Good at Reads and range scans Very high write rates
Found in PostgreSQL, MySQL Cassandra, RocksDB

Remember it as: ask the database for its plan; if it is walking every aisle, put up a sign that matches the question.

◷How we got hereIn 1970 Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight, at Boeing's research laboratory, had an index too large for memory…

In 1970 Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight, at Boeing's research laboratory, had an index too large for memory and a disk that was slow to seek. Their answer, published in 1972, was a tree with very wide nodes, each the size of a disk page, so that any key is a handful of page reads away; they called it the B-tree and never said what the B stood for. It has been the default index for fifty years. Its weakness is that every write lands on a different page. Patrick O'Neil and three colleagues described the log-structured merge tree in 1996 for tables that are written far more than read, such as histories, trading random writes for sequential ones and a background merge. The write-heavy stores of the 2000s were built on it.

⚠The traps
  • An index for every column: the sign is a table with more indexes than queries, added "to be safe". Every write pays for all of them and the useful ones are pushed out of memory.
  • Offset pagination at depth: the sign is OFFSET with a number supplied by the client. Latency grows with the page number, and a crawler walking to page 10,000 becomes a table scan.
  • N+1 queries: the sign is a query inside a loop over the results of another query, often hidden by an object mapper. One page becomes dozens of round trips.
  • The unbounded query: the sign is a SELECT with no LIMIT on a table that grows. It works for the customer with ten orders and takes the database down for the customer with thirty thousand.
  • Pool exhaustion: the sign is requests failing with "timed out waiting for a connection" while the database's processors are not full. Slow queries are holding every connection, and fast ones starve.
◉Spot it

Fulfilment lists the paid orders awaiting dispatch, oldest first:

SELECT o.id, o.placed_at, o.total_minor
  FROM orders o
 WHERE o.status = 'PAID'
   AND o.placed_at < '2026-08-01'
 ORDER BY o.placed_at
 LIMIT 50;

CREATE INDEX orders_paid ON orders (placed_at, status);
Show the answer

Answer The index columns are in the wrong order. The sign is the range column first and the equality column second: the index is sorted by date across every status, so the database must walk all the entries before August and discard the delivered ones, which is nearly all of them. The fix is (status, placed_at), which jumps to the paid orders and reads them already in date order.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. For the three most frequent queries, what does the plan say: which index, and how many rows read?
  2. How many database connections can all the app servers open together, and what is the database's limit?
  3. What is the largest result any one query can return, and what bounds it?

Still argued: which storage engine should be the default. Siying Dong and colleagues at Facebook (2017) report moving their main MySQL workload from a B-tree engine to an LSM-tree one and halving the storage it used, with fewer writes to flash. For large write-heavy datasets, they argue, the LSM-tree is simply more efficient. Goetz Graefe's survey Modern B-Tree Techniques (2011) sets out how far B-trees have been optimised for modern hardware. The case for them is predictable reads: one path down the tree, and no background merge to stall behind. Manos Athanassoulis and others (2016) put the disagreement as a conjecture: an engine can minimise read cost, update cost or space, but not all three. Most teams never choose, because the database they picked chose for them.

What Ana learned

  • Read the plan for every query on a page before that page meets a load test.
  • Create the index the query needs, with equality columns first, and remove the ones nothing uses.
  • Count connections across the whole fleet, give the pool a timeout, and bound every result.

…but

With the index in place the test passes 800 and keeps going. The arithmetic is less kind. Catalogue's database must answer 10,000 queries a second at the sale peak, 99% of them reads, and the test puts one machine's comfortable limit near 6,000. It is also still one machine, in Zone A.

Chapter 5 · Act IICopies of the Stock Book#

The problem

Two numbers and one fright.

The numbers are from chapter 4: Catalogue's database must answer 10,000 queries a second at the sale peak, and one machine is comfortable at about 6,000. Nearly all of those queries are reads. The indexes are right; there is simply more reading to do than one machine can do.

The fright comes on a Wednesday afternoon, when the disk controller in Ordering's database machine starts logging errors. Nothing is lost. But Kofi asks the room how long it would take to rebuild that database on a new machine, and nobody knows, because it has never been done. The only other copy of Bramble's orders is last night's backup, taken at 02:00. Had the disk died at four in the afternoon, fourteen hours of orders, some thirty thousand of them, paid for and not yet shipped, would have existed nowhere.

Priya's proposal covers the first problem: a nightly copy of the catalogue onto a second machine, and send the product pages there. Ana sees what is wrong with it before Kofi says anything. A copy made at night is a day old by evening, and it does nothing for an order placed this afternoon. What Bramble needs is a copy that is at most a moment behind, kept that way continuously, on a machine that can take over.

The idea

Replication is copying the stock book to other depots, continuously. One machine is the leader: the head office book, where every write is made. The others are followers: branch copies. The mechanism is chapter 4's goods-in book. The leader already appends every change to its write-ahead log; it now also ships that log to each follower, and each follower applies the same changes in the same order.

That gives two things at once. A follower can answer reads, so it is a read replica: a leader and two followers offer three machines' worth of reading. And a follower holds everything the leader has, or nearly, so one can be promoted if the leader dies. What replication does not give is more writing: every follower must apply every write, so write capacity stays that of one machine.

"Or nearly" is the whole subject. It depends on whether the leader waits.

Synchronous Asynchronous
The leader says "committed" After the follower confirms it has the change As soon as its own log is written
If the leader dies No acknowledged write is lost The last unshipped writes are lost
Cost Each write waits a round trip; a dead follower stalls writes None on the write path
Usual compromise One follower synchronous, in another zone The rest, used for reads

An asynchronous follower is always a little behind. Replication lag is the copy that arrives on the evening van: usually milliseconds, and seconds or minutes when the leader is busy, which is exactly when most people are reading. Here the depot picture needs a warning. A box of notebooks is in one depot or another. A record can be in three places at once and slightly out of date in two of them. The book is copied; the stock is not.

Lag produces two anomalies that customers notice.

The customer has just paid and the shop says they have not. Some of them order again. The guarantee they needed is read-your-writes: after your own write, you see it. The cheap way to provide it is to send a customer's reads to the leader for a few seconds after they write; the precise way is to remember the log position of their write and read only from a copy that has reached it. Everyone else's reads may be stale; yours may not.

The second anomaly is time running backwards. A customer refreshes twice, the first read lands on a follower that is up to date and the second on one that is behind, and an order appears and then vanishes. Monotonic reads means never seeing older data than you have already seen, and the simple way to get it is to send each customer to the same follower every time.

Failover is a branch becoming head office. Something must notice the leader has gone, choose the follower with the most complete log, promote it, point the app servers at it, and make sure the old leader does not come back still believing it leads. Each step has a failure of its own. Declare the leader dead too quickly and a slow moment causes a failover; too slowly and the shop is closed for minutes. Promote an asynchronous follower and its missing writes are gone. And if the old leader returns unaware, there are two branches both believing they are head office, each accepting writes the other never sees. That is split brain, and chapter 14 is about preventing it properly. For now Bramble uses the database's own failover manager, with the synchronous follower as the only candidate, and rehearses it.

This chapter's design has one leader. Two others exist and Act IV meets both: multi-leader, where several machines accept writes and conflicts must be resolved, and leaderless, where any copy accepts a write and a reader asks several copies and takes the newest.

Use a single leader with followers by default. The rule gives way when writes must be accepted in two places that cannot always reach each other, and the price is conflict resolution, which is most of chapter 13.

Remember it as: one head office book, copied to the branches; a branch may be a moment behind, so never read your own entry from a branch.

◷How we got hereDatabases have shipped their logs to standby machines since the 1980s, but for most teams replication arrived…

Databases have shipped their logs to standby machines since the 1980s, but for most teams replication arrived with the open-source databases: MySQL gained it in 2000 and it became the standard way to scale a website's reads; PostgreSQL built streaming replication in 2010. The trouble it causes was named early. Douglas Terry and colleagues at Xerox PARC, building a store for laptops that were often disconnected, defined "read your writes" and "monotonic reads" in 1994 as guarantees a session could ask for when the copies disagreed. The vocabulary reached working engineers through Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications in 2017, whose replication chapter set single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless side by side and listed what goes wrong in a failover. It reacted to a decade of teams adding replicas for speed and discovering the anomalies in production.

⚠The traps
  • Reading your own write from a replica: the sign is a page shown immediately after a write whose query goes to a follower. The customer's own change is missing, and they repeat it.
  • The failover never tested: the sign is a failover described in a document and never carried out on purpose. The first run happens during an outage and finds the step nobody automated.
  • Asynchronous replication assumed durable: the sign is a claim that "no committed data is lost" over a design with only asynchronous followers. Whatever the leader acknowledged and had not yet shipped disappears with it.
  • The replica as backup: the sign is "we have replicas" given as the answer to "what if someone deletes the table?". The mistake is copied to every follower within a second; only a copy from the past, kept apart, undoes it.
◉Spot it

A note on the orders database: "The leader is in Zone A with one follower in Zone B, replicating asynchronously so that writes stay fast. If the leader misses heartbeats for thirty seconds, the failover manager powers it off, promotes the follower and repoints the app servers. We rehearse this every quarter. Order confirmation pages read from the leader. With this design, no order a customer has seen confirmed can be lost if Zone A fails."

Show the answer

Answer The last sentence is false. The sign is the word "asynchronously" next to "no order can be lost": an order the leader confirmed in the instant before Zone A failed may never have reached Zone B. The fix is to make the Zone B follower synchronous, accepting a round trip between zones on every write, or to state honestly how many seconds of orders may be lost. The rest of the note is sound.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What does a customer see in the second after their own write, and which copy served it?
  2. If the leader dies now, how many acknowledged writes can be lost, and how long until writes are accepted again?
  3. When was failover last carried out on purpose, and what stops the old leader returning as a leader?

Still argued: whether failover should be automatic. Google's Site Reliability Engineering (2016) describes automating database failover until it completed in seconds without a person. The argument is that humans are slow, are asleep, and make mistakes under pressure that a tested program does not. GitHub's analysis of its outage of October 2018 describes an automatic failover that, after a network break of forty-three seconds, promoted databases in another region and left each side holding writes the other lacked. Service was degraded for a day while data was restored, and the company afterwards reconfigured its failover tool never to promote a database in another region. Both automate detection and the mechanics. They differ on how far a program's decision should be allowed to reach, and the cases that divide them are the ambiguous ones, where the leader is slow or unreachable but not dead.

What Ana learned

  • Send writes to one leader, reads to followers, and a customer's own reads to the leader for a few seconds after they write.
  • Keep one synchronous follower in another zone and say in writing what an asynchronous one can lose.
  • Rehearse failover on a schedule, and keep backups as well as replicas.

…but

On the first Friday with replicas, Fulfilment reports an order for a notebook that is not on the shelf: two customers each bought the last one. Priya blames the follower that served the stock check and moves that read to the leader. The following Monday it happens again.

Chapter 6 · Act IITwo Clerks, One Shelf#

The problem

The Juniper A5 is a hand-bound notebook from a seller who makes them one at a time. On Friday at 12:04 there is one in stock. At 12:04:07 a customer in Leeds buys it. At 12:04:07 a customer in Cardiff also buys it. Both are charged, both receive a confirmation, and Fulfilment's picker finds one notebook and two packing slips.

Priya's theory was replication lag: the stock check had read a stale follower. She moved it to the leader, and on Monday it happened again with a fountain pen. So the copies are not the cause. Both customers read the true, current stock level from the same machine, and it was still wrong to act on.

Ana reads the code. It is four lines and each is reasonable. Read the stock level. If it is at least one, carry on. Take payment. Write the stock level back as one less than the value read. She traces two checkouts through those four lines on the whiteboard, interleaved, and the bug is in the gap between the first line and the last. Nothing in the code is wrong for one customer. It is wrong for two.

Kofi has a name for the four lines: check-then-act. He has a second observation, which is that Bramble has been running this code for three years, and the reason it has started failing now is that there are finally enough customers to arrive in the same second.

The idea

Here is the interleaving. Read it the way a picker would replay a mistake.

This is a lost update: two clerks each selling the last box. B's write was computed from a value that A had already changed, and A's sale vanished under it. The tool for preventing it is as old as databases.

A transaction is one clerk's complete stock movement: a group of reads and writes the database treats as a unit. Its promises are abbreviated ACID. Atomicity: all of it happens or none of it does. Consistency: it takes the data from one valid state to another, where "valid" means rules the application declares, such as available >= 0. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work. Durability: once committed, it survives a crash, which is the write-ahead log's job.

Bramble's code ran inside a transaction and oversold anyway, because isolation is not one promise. It is a dial, and isolation in the depot is how much one clerk sees of another's half-finished count. Each setting permits some anomalies:

Isolation level Dirty read Lost update Write skew Phantom
Read committed Cannot occur Can occur Can occur Can occur
Snapshot isolation Cannot occur Cannot occur; MySQL's repeatable read is weaker and allows it Can occur Cannot occur in reads; can cause write skew
Serializable Cannot occur Cannot occur Cannot occur Cannot occur

A dirty read is seeing a change that has not been committed and may be rolled back. A lost update is the notebook. Write skew is two clerks each checking the rota and both going home: each reads the same facts, each makes a decision that is safe alone, and they write different rows, so nothing is overwritten and the rule ("one first-aider on shift") is broken anyway. A phantom is a row that appears in another transaction's search after it has looked: two checkouts each count a customer's purchases of a one-per-person item, find none, and each insert one.

The levels are built on multi-version concurrency control: the database keeps several versions of each row, and a reader sees a snapshot from a moment in the past instead of waiting for writers. Snapshot isolation gives a transaction one snapshot for its whole life (PostgreSQL calls this level "repeatable read"). Serializable guarantees the result equals some one-at-a-time order, and pays for it by aborting transactions that would break that, which the application must retry.

PostgreSQL's default is read committed. So is Oracle's. Bramble's code needed more than its database was set to give. There are three fixes.

Pessimistic lock Optimistic lock
Picture Roping off the aisle Checking the shelf label has not changed before you write
Mechanism Lock the row when reading; others wait Write only if the row is still as expected; otherwise fail
Best when Conflicts are frequent Conflicts are rare
Cost Waiting, and deadlocks Retries, or telling the customer no 
-- What the code did: check, then act, with a gap between
SELECT available FROM stock WHERE sku = 'NB-JUNIPER-A5';     -- both read 1
UPDATE stock SET available = 0 WHERE sku = 'NB-JUNIPER-A5';  -- both write 0

-- Pessimistic: the locking read
BEGIN;
SELECT available FROM stock
 WHERE sku = 'NB-JUNIPER-A5'
   FOR UPDATE;                  -- the second checkout waits here
UPDATE stock SET available = available - 1, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
 WHERE sku = 'NB-JUNIPER-A5';   -- run only if the value read was at least 1
COMMIT;

The locking read works and makes every checkout for that item queue. The better fix removes the gap by making the check and the act one statement:

UPDATE stock
   SET available = available - 1, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
 WHERE sku = 'NB-JUNIPER-A5'
   AND available >= 1;
-- 1 row updated: the notebook is yours.
-- 0 rows updated: someone took the last one; say "sold out".

This conditional update is the optimistic lock in its smallest form. The database applies it to one checkout at a time, and the caller learns that it lost from the count of rows changed: zero means sold out, and no payment is taken. The third fix, raising the level to serializable, also works, at the cost of retrying aborted transactions everywhere; Bramble keeps it for the few places where a rule spans several rows.

Locks bring one new failure. An order for a pen and a pad locks the pen row and then the pad row; another order locks the pad and then the pen. Each waits for the other for ever. That is a deadlock. The database detects it and kills one, which must retry. Lock rows in one agreed order, such as by sku, and it cannot form.

Remember it as: never read, decide and then write; make the check and the change one statement, and let the count of rows tell you who lost.

◷How we got hereJim Gray's 1981 paper "The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations" described a transaction as a…

Jim Gray's 1981 paper "The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations" described a transaction as a contract, with consistency, atomicity and durability as its terms, drawing on what IBM's database projects had built in the 1970s. Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter added isolation and coined the acronym ACID in 1983. The SQL standard of 1992 then defined four isolation levels by the anomalies each forbids, and vendors implemented them differently. In 1995 Hal Berenson, Gray and four others published "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels", showing the standard's definitions were ambiguous, that they missed lost update and write skew altogether, and that the snapshot isolation several products shipped fitted none of the names. That paper reacted to a market in which "serializable" on the box did not always mean serializable, and it is the reason the table above has the columns it has.

⚠The traps
  • Check-then-act: the sign is a read, an if in application code, then a write that depends on the read. Two requests pass the check together and both act.
  • Assuming the default isolation level is serializable: the sign is a design that says "it's in a transaction, so it's safe" and names no level. Most databases default to read committed, which permits lost updates and write skew.
  • The long transaction: the sign is a network call, a file upload or user thinking time between BEGIN and COMMIT. Locks and old row versions are held for seconds, and everything touching those rows queues.
  • Inconsistent lock order: the sign is two code paths that lock the same rows in different orders. They deadlock under load, and only under load.
◉Spot it

Checkout for a pen, rewritten after the Juniper incident. The application checks that the value read is at least 1 before continuing.

BEGIN;
SELECT available FROM stock
 WHERE sku = 'PEN-FINE-BLK'
   FOR UPDATE;
-- the application calls the payment provider here and waits for its answer
UPDATE stock SET available = available - 1, updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
 WHERE sku = 'PEN-FINE-BLK';
COMMIT;
Show the answer

Answer The row lock is held across the call to the payment provider. The sign is a network call between BEGIN and COMMIT: when the provider takes forty seconds, every other checkout for that pen waits forty seconds, and the connection pool drains behind them. The stock logic is correct. The fix is to reserve the stock with a conditional update in a short transaction, take payment outside any transaction, and release the reservation if payment fails.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which isolation level does this transaction run at, and was that chosen or inherited from the default?
  2. Where is there a read followed by a write that depends on it, and what stops another transaction between them?
  3. What is the longest a transaction holds a lock, and is any network call made inside it?

Still argued: whether serializable should be the default. Todd Warszawski and Peter Bailis (2017) examined a dozen popular e-commerce applications and found all but one could be made to oversell stock, overspend vouchers or alter a basket through concurrent requests at the databases' default levels. Five of their twenty-two flaws would be closed by serializable isolation; the rest came from code that split one operation across transactions, which no level repairs, and they argue that developers cannot be expected to find such flaws unaided. Bailis and others (2014) showed that many invariants, such as foreign keys and counters that only increase, hold without any coordination between transactions, and that enforcing serializability for them costs throughput and availability for nothing. The first position asks for safety by default and opt-out for speed. The second asks for speed by default and coordination only where an invariant needs it. That the two papers share an author says how real the trade-off is.

What Ana learned

  • Find every read-then-write in the code and turn it into one conditional statement or a locking read.
  • Write the isolation level into the design, and name the anomaly each sensitive transaction must not suffer.
  • Keep transactions short, with no network call inside, and take locks in one order.

…but

Stock is right. The orders table is now the problem: 40 million orders and 120 million lines, about 150 GB with indexes on a machine with 64 GB of memory. The nightly backup takes six hours, changing a column's type takes the table away for most of a morning, and Marcus, the consultant, has a proposal to split it across four databases.

Chapter 7 · Act IIToo Big for One Depot#

The problem

Ordering's database holds 40 million orders and 120 million order lines: about 150 GB with indexes, on a machine with 64 GB of memory. Tables and indexes together no longer fit in memory, so a lookup for an old order goes to disk. The nightly backup takes six hours. Changing a column's type rewrites the table and takes most of a morning.

Priya's instinct was more memory. Marcus, the consultant Lena calls when the system creaks, proposed something larger, and Priya has built it in the test environment over two weeks: four databases, with each order stored in database number hash(customer_id) % 4. Placing an order is as fast as ever. She demonstrates it on a Thursday and Kofi asks for a week to try to break it.

It takes three days. An office-supplies reseller places 8% of all Bramble's orders, 4,000 a day, and whichever database holds that customer does a third more work than the others. Fulfilment's screen of unshipped orders, which has no customer in its query, now asks all four databases and waits for the slowest. And when Kofi adds a fifth database to see what growing looks like, % 4 becomes % 5, and four orders in every five are suddenly in the wrong place. Moving them takes the weekend.

Nothing in the design is wrong, exactly. Each of those three things is what partitioning is, and Ana wants to know which of them Bramble is obliged to live with.

The idea

Chapter 5 put the same data on several machines. This chapter puts different data on each.

Replication Partitioning
Each machine holds A copy of everything Its own share
Buys Read capacity and survival Write capacity and room
Costs Lag between copies Queries and transactions that span shares

Partitioning, which most engineers call sharding when the shares are on different machines, is splitting stock across depots. The partition key is the rule that says which depot holds which box, and choosing it is the whole design. A query that includes the key goes to one partition. A query that does not must ask them all.

There are two ways to turn a key into a partition. Range partitioning gives each partition a span of keys: orders by month, customers by first letter. Neighbouring keys live together, so a scan across a range is cheap, and the spans must be chosen so that load is even. Hash partitioning runs the key through a hash function and assigns by the result. Load spreads evenly whatever the keys look like, and range scans are lost.

Each of Kofi's three findings has a name.

Hash modulo N and rebalancing. With hash % N, changing N reassigns almost every key: going from four to five keeps a key in place only when both remainders agree, which is one time in five. Consistent hashing fixes this. Picture the hash values as a ring. Each node is placed at many points on it, and a key belongs to the first node point at or after its own hash. Adding a node takes over only the slices just before its points: about one key in five moves when a fifth node joins, and none of them moves between old nodes. It is redrawing depot territories so that only a few streets change hands.

public final class HashRing {
    private static final int POINTS_PER_NODE = 100;   // many points even out the slices
    private final NavigableMap<Long, String> ring = new TreeMap<>();

    public void add(String node) {
        for (int i = 0; i < POINTS_PER_NODE; i++) ring.put(hash(node + "#" + i), node);
    }
    public void remove(String node) {
        ring.values().removeIf(node::equals);
    }
    /** The owner of a key: the first point at or after its hash, wrapping round. */
    public String nodeFor(String partitionKey) {
        var point = ring.ceilingEntry(hash(partitionKey));
        return (point != null ? point : ring.firstEntry()).getValue();
    }
    private static long hash(String s) {
        try {
            byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
                                         .digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            return ByteBuffer.wrap(digest).getLong();   // the first 8 bytes are enough
        } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
    }
}

Rebalancing is the moving itself. Systems that do it well fix a large number of small partitions at the start, say 1,024, and move whole partitions between machines, at a time an operator chooses.

Hot keys and skew. Hashing spreads keys evenly. It does not spread load evenly when one key is busier than the rest. The reseller is a hot key: the one box everybody wants, in one depot. The remedies are to split that key further (the reseller's orders by month), to serve it from a cache, or to give it a partition of its own.

Scatter-gather. A query without the partition key is sent to every partition and the answers merged. It is as slow as the slowest partition, and chapter 1's tail arithmetic applies: with four partitions, a one-in-a-hundred slow response becomes one in twenty-five. Secondary indexes face the same choice. A local index lives in each partition and covers only its rows, so writes are cheap and reads by that index scatter. A global index covers all partitions and is itself partitioned, so reads go to one place and every write touches two.

One more cost. A seller's payout that marks forty customers' orders as settled now changes rows on several machines, and doing that atomically is a cross-partition transaction: it needs a commit protocol across machines, or a saga, which the Atlas covers in chapter 16. Choose a key so that things changed together share it.

All of this is the price. So the rule is to try everything cheaper before you shard, in this order: delete or archive what nobody reads; fix the queries and indexes; buy a bigger machine; add read replicas; partition inside one database. The last is what Bramble does. PostgreSQL can split a table by range into child tables on the same machine, and Ordering's tables are now partitioned by month. The current month is 1.5 million orders and its index fits in memory. Old months are read-only, backed up once and never rewritten.

And the number at which Marcus's design becomes right: the leader comfortably takes 5,000 row writes a second, an order is about ten rows, so one machine is good for some 500 orders a second. The sale peaks at 20. Sharding across machines is warranted near 500 orders a second sustained, or when a month of data outgrows one machine.

Remember it as: choose the rule that says which depot holds which box, and put things that change together in the same depot.

◷How we got hereMichael Stonebraker's 1986 paper "The Case for Shared Nothing" argued that databases should scale across…

Michael Stonebraker's 1986 paper "The Case for Shared Nothing" argued that databases should scale across machines that share neither memory nor disk, each owning a slice of the data, and the parallel databases of the next decade were built that way. The method of assigning slices came from elsewhere. In 1997 David Karger and colleagues at MIT published consistent hashing to solve a problem of web caching: how to spread pages over a set of cache servers that changes, without every server's contents becoming wrong at once. A decade later Amazon's Dynamo used the same ring to place data, and the large websites of the 2000s, having outgrown single databases, hand-built partitioning into their applications and called the pieces shards. Each step reacted to the same wall: a machine that could not be made bigger.

⚠The traps
  • Sharding too early: the sign is a partitioning design with no figure for the write rate or data size one machine could not take. The team pays for scatter-gather and cross-partition transactions years before it needs to.
  • The monotonic partition key: the sign is range partitioning on a timestamp or a counter in order to spread writes. Every new row belongs to the newest partition, which takes all the load while the rest idle.
  • The hot partition: the sign is one partition at full utilisation while the others are quiet. A single busy key lives there, and adding machines does not help.
  • Hash modulo N: the sign is hash(key) % numberOfNodes in routing code. Changing the number of nodes moves nearly all the data.
  • Routine cross-partition transactions: the sign is an everyday operation that must change rows in two partitions atomically. The partition key separates things that change together, and every such write is slow and fragile.
◉Spot it

A design note for the stock-movement history: "The table records every change to every stock level and is written far more than it is read. To spread the write load, it is range-partitioned by movement timestamp across four machines, each holding one quarter of the year. Each partition has a synchronous follower in another zone. Every query includes a time range. A new machine is added each quarter."

Show the answer

Answer The partition key is the timestamp, so every write goes to the machine holding the current quarter and the other three take none. The sign is range partitioning on a value that only increases, offered as a way to spread writes. The fix is to hash on sku so that writes spread across machines, to order by time inside each partition, and to accept that a query by time range then asks every machine. Partitioning by time is a sound way to archive; it does not share load.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What is the partition key, and which frequent queries do not include it?
  2. What share of the load goes to the busiest key, and what does its partition look like at peak?
  3. When a machine is added, what fraction of the data moves, and who decides when?

Still argued: whether the application or the database should do the sharding. Marty Weiner's account of Pinterest's MySQL fleet (2015) argues for sharding in the application: the routing is a few lines the team fully understands, each shard is an ordinary database with ordinary tools, and nothing clever can fail at night. Jeff Shute and colleagues, describing Google's F1 database (2013), report the opposite experience: hand-sharded MySQL made rebalancing so painful and cross-shard work so awkward that they moved the advertising business to a database that partitions itself and offers transactions across partitions. The first accepts limits on queries in exchange for simplicity. The second accepts a far more complex database, and slower writes, in exchange for an application that does not know the data is split.

What Ana learned

  • Before agreeing to partition, write down the write rate and data size one machine cannot take, and compare them with today's.
  • Choose the partition key from the queries, so that the frequent ones name it and things that change together share it.
  • Ask for the busiest key's share of load before trusting any even-spread diagram.

…but

Orders are in monthly partitions and fit their machine again. Catalogue is next. A search for "dotted notebook A5" takes six seconds, the catalogue backup is a little over 200 GB, nearly all of it photographs, and Marcus has a second slide, proposing that Bramble replace all its databases with one partitioned store.

Chapter 8 · Act IIA Shelf for Every Kind of Thing#

The problem

Lena types "dotted notebook A5" into Bramble's search box during a board meeting and waits six seconds. The query behind it is LIKE '%dotted%' across the names and descriptions of 200,000 products. No B-tree helps: an index is sorted from the first letter, and this asks for a word in the middle, so the database reads every description, every time.

The same week, restoring the catalogue to a test machine takes four hours. The backup is a little over 200 GB. Product text accounts for less than half a gigabyte of it. The rest is the photographs, a million of them, stored in a column of the products table since the first version of the shop and sent to browsers through database connections.

Marcus's new slide has one box on it. Replace the relational databases with a single partitioned key-value store, as Amazon did: no leader to fail over, no schema to migrate, capacity added a node at a time, writes accepted even when machines are down. Priya, who spent a morning last month waiting for a column to be changed, is half persuaded.

Ana notices that the proposal answers neither the search nor the photographs. It answers a question about write volume that nobody at Bramble has asked.

The idea

A depot has shelving, bins, a cold room and a barn, each built for one kind of goods. Datastores are the same, and the way to choose one is to write down the access pattern first: how the data is read (by key, by range, by word, by relationship), how fast it is written, how big it gets, and what must always be true of it.

Family Shape Good at Poor at Examples
Relational Rows in tables, joined on demand Questions nobody predicted; rules across rows; transactions Write rates beyond one leader PostgreSQL, MySQL
Key-value A value fetched by its key Very fast reads and writes by key: sessions, baskets Any question not by key Redis, DynamoDB
Document store Self-contained documents by id Reading and writing one whole thing; varied attributes Joins; rules across documents MongoDB
Wide-column Rows grouped by partition key, sorted within it Enormous write volumes; time-ordered data per key Ad-hoc queries; joins Cassandra, Bigtable
Graph Nodes and the edges between them Questions many hops long Bulk totals Neo4j
Search index Words pointing to documents Text search, ranking, filters Being the record of anything Elasticsearch, Lucene
Time-series Values keyed by time Metrics; ranges over time; compaction of old data Updates in place Prometheus, InfluxDB
Object storage Large blobs by key, over HTTP Images, backups, files fetched whole; very cheap Queries; partial updates S3 and its equivalents

A search index is the catalogue you can look up by any word on the label. It is built on an inverted index: for every word, a sorted list of the products that contain it. "Dotted notebook A5" becomes three lists intersected, which takes milliseconds, and ranking and spelling tolerance come with it. It is fed from the catalogue database, a moment behind, and can be rebuilt from it at any time. That last property is the rule: the search index answers questions and owns nothing.

Object storage is the bulk barn: big things, fetched whole, by ticket. The photographs move there, the products table keeps only each one's key, and the browser fetches the image directly.

Using several kinds of store, each for what it does well, is polyglot persistence, and it has a price the table does not show. Every store is one more thing to back up, upgrade, monitor, secure and be paged for. And the same fact now lives in two places, the database and the search index, which must be kept in step and will sometimes disagree. The test is this: a new store earns its place when a question cannot be answered by the store you have, and not before.

Document and key-value stores are called schemaless. The data still has a shape; the store has merely stopped checking it. The schema moves into every piece of code that reads the data, which must now cope with every shape ever written.

Now Marcus. His argument is the one Amazon made for its shopping basket: adding an item must succeed even when disks fail and data centres are cut off, because a rejected write is a lost sale, and so the store accepts writes at any node and reconciles the differences afterwards. It is a real design, built for a service taking tens of millions of requests a day at the peak, and everything he says about it is true. Three numbers answer him.

Bramble's sale peak is 20 orders a second, about 200 row writes; one leader comfortably takes 5,000, so Bramble is using 4% of one machine's writing. Its data is 150 GB; the machine holds 1 TB. And a rehearsed failover closes writes for about thirty seconds, a few times a year, which Lena accepts. The premise of Marcus's store is that even that is too much. In exchange it gives up joins, transactions across rows and the conditional update of chapter 6: a store that accepts writes on both sides of a failure cannot promise that the last notebook is sold once.

So the answer is "not yet", with the figures at which it changes: sustained writes near 500 orders a second, or a business that would sooner sell the notebook twice than refuse a sale. And Marcus is right about one thing today. A basket is exactly the data he describes, fetched by key, merged without harm. Bramble's baskets have lived in a key-value store since chapter 3.
