Remember it as: write down the questions before choosing the shelf; keep one book of record, and let every other store be a copy you could rebuild.

◷How we got hereEdgar Codd's 1970 paper "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" proposed that data be kept…

Edgar Codd's 1970 paper "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" proposed that data be kept in tables and queried by what it is, not by where it is stored. It reacted to databases in which every program had to know the path from one record to the next, so that reorganising the data broke the programs. Relational databases then ruled for thirty years, until two companies outgrew them. Google described Bigtable in 2006, a sorted, wide-column store spread over thousands of machines, and Amazon described Dynamo in 2007, a key-value store that stays writable through failures by giving up consistency. Open-source imitations followed within two years under the banner "NoSQL".

⚠The traps
  • A database chosen by fashion: the sign is a store selected before anyone has listed the queries or the write rate. The team inherits the limits of a design built for a problem it does not have.
  • Polyglot sprawl: the sign is a new kind of store with each new feature and no owner for its backups. Operating cost and the number of ways data can disagree grow with every one.
  • The search index as source of truth: the sign is a write that goes to the search index first, or data that exists nowhere else. Indexes are rebuilt and lag; whatever only they hold is eventually lost.
  • Blobs in the database: the sign is a column of images or documents in a transactional table. Backups, replication and memory are spent on bytes the database never queries.
  • Schemaless meaning no schema: the sign is "we don't need migrations" beside reading code full of checks for missing fields. The schema still exists, unwritten, in every reader.
◉Spot it

The flow for a seller editing a product, after search was added:

Show the answer

Answer The product is written to the search index and copied to the database afterwards. The sign is an arrow of writes pointing at the index and a dashed arrow pointing from it to the system of record: the index has become the source of truth, a rebuild loses a day of edits, and product pages are up to a day stale. The fix is to write to the database and feed the index from it.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What are the three most frequent questions asked of this data, and is each by key, by range, by word or by relationship?
  2. Which store is the record for each fact, and can every other store be rebuilt from it?
  3. Who backs up, upgrades and is paged for the new store, and have they agreed?

Still argued: one general database or several special ones. Michael Stonebraker and Uğur Çetintemel's "One Size Fits All: An Idea Whose Time Has Come and Gone" (2005) argues that a general relational engine is beaten tenfold by engines built for one workload, and Martin Fowler's note on polyglot persistence (2011) drew the conclusion for applications: use each store for what it is best at. Dan McKinley's "Choose Boring Technology" (2015) argues that every new technology spends a limited budget of attention, that the cost of operating a store dwarfs the cost of adopting it, and that a team should stretch what it already runs well before adding anything. The first side measures the engine. The second measures the team.

What Ana learned

  • List the access patterns before naming a product, and move a workload to a new store only when the current one cannot answer a question.
  • Keep one system of record per fact and make every other store rebuildable from it.
  • Answer a proposal built for another company's scale with your own write rate, data size and tolerance for a refused write.

…but

Search is fast and the database is small. In the sale rehearsal, though, every product page still asks the database the same five questions: 10,000 queries a second for content that changes twice a day. Two followers carry 5,000 queries a second each, close to their comfortable 6,000 and with nothing spare if one fails, and Priya has ordered three more to re-read the same rows.

Chapter 9 · Act IIIThe Shelf by the Counter#

The problem

The sale rehearsal passes, narrowly. Every product page asks the database five questions, so 2,000 pages a second is 10,000 queries a second, and the answers change about twice a day. The followers sit close to their limit, re-reading the same rows.

Priya's fix goes live on a Monday: each app server keeps the pages it has built in a map in its own memory and serves them from there. The followers fall quiet. On Tuesday a week of 20% off the weekly planner ends. Some customers see £10, some still see £8, depending on which of the twelve servers answers, and those who see £8 are charged £10 at checkout, because checkout reads the database. Nothing ever removes an entry from the map. Restarting all twelve servers fixes the price and, for four minutes, sends every request back to the database at once.

Version two uses one shared cache and expires every entry after sixty seconds. The prices are right within a minute. But the database graph now has teeth: quiet, then a spike, every sixty seconds exactly. At 09:00:00 in the rehearsal the planner's entry expires, and the three hundred requests that arrive for it in the next second each find nothing, and each run the five queries.

Kofi says both versions are the classic ones, and that the shelf is the easy part. Knowing when to restock it is the design.

The idea

A cache is the shelf by the counter: answers already worked out, kept where they are quick to reach. Chapter 2's table is the reason it pays. Memory is a thousand times faster than disk, and a cached page costs one lookup instead of five queries.

There are four ways to wire a cache to a database, and they differ in who talks to the database and when.

Pattern On a read On a write Risk
Cache-aside The application looks in the cache; on a miss it reads the database and fills the cache The application writes the database and deletes the entry A stale entry if the delete is missed
Read-through The application asks only the cache, which loads from the database on a miss As cache-aside The same, hidden inside the cache
Write-through Served from the cache The cache writes the database before confirming Slower writes; caches things never read
Write-behind Served from the cache The cache confirms at once and writes the database later Writes lost if the cache dies first

Bramble uses cache-aside, the commonest and the easiest to reason about. Five decisions make it safe.

When does an entry leave? Three ways. Its time to live runs out: the date after which you restock it. It is removed by invalidation: pulling an item off the shelf when the aisle price changes, which here means that when Catalogue or Promotions changes a product they delete its entry. Or it is evicted because memory is full, and the usual policy drops the least recently used. Use the first two together. Invalidation makes changes prompt; the time to live catches the deletes that were missed. Never cache without an expiry. The exception is content that cannot change, keyed by a version, which may be kept for ever at no cost.

What happens when a popular entry expires? A cache stampede: every clerk running to the same aisle when the counter shelf empties.

The fix is single-flight: for each key, one caller loads and the rest wait for its answer. Add a little randomness to each time to live so that entries filled together do not expire together.

public final class ProductPages {
    private final PageCache cache;        // get(sku), put(sku, page, ttl)
    private final PageLoader loader;      // the five queries
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<Sku, CompletableFuture<ProductPage>> loading =
            new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public ProductPages(PageCache cache, PageLoader loader) {
        this.cache = cache; this.loader = loader;
    }
    public ProductPage get(Sku sku) {
        Optional<ProductPage> hit = cache.get(sku);            // cache-aside: the shelf first
        if (hit.isPresent()) return hit.get();
        var load = loading.computeIfAbsent(sku, k ->           // single-flight: one loader per sku
                CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> cache.get(k).orElseGet(() -> {
                    ProductPage page = loader.load(k);         // re-checked: a load may just have ended
                    cache.put(k, page, ttlWithJitter());
                    return page;
                })));
        try { return load.join(); }                            // everyone else waits for it
        finally { loading.remove(sku, load); }
    }
    private static Duration ttlWithJitter() {                  // five minutes, give or take 30 s
        return Duration.ofSeconds(270 + ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(61));
    }
}

This protects each server. Across twelve servers the planner page is loaded at most twelve times, not three hundred.

What about things that do not exist? A request for a product that was deleted misses the cache every time and reaches the database every time. Negative caching stores "no such product" for a short while, so that a crawler walking dead links does not become a query load.

Where does the cache live? A local cache is in each server's memory: no network hop, but twelve copies that disagree, each empty after every deploy. A distributed cache is a separate cluster all servers share: one copy, half a millisecond away, still warm after a deploy, and one more thing that can fail. Its keys are spread over its nodes by chapter 7's ring. Bramble uses the distributed one, for the reason Tuesday demonstrated.

How do you know it is working? The hit ratio is the share of reads served from the cache. At 95%, the database sees 500 of the 10,000 queries a second. The figure is touchier than it looks: falling from 99% to 98% doubles what reaches the database.

One thing a cache cannot give is the truth. It is a copy, and its consistency with the database is only ever approximate: a reader can fetch an old row, lose a race with a writer's delete, and put the old row back until the time to live removes it. So nothing is decided from the cache. The price charged and the stock sold are read from the system of record, by chapter 6's conditional update, every time.

Remember it as: keep answers on the shelf by the counter, date every one, pull it when the aisle changes, and never price a sale from it.

◷How we got hereIn 2003 Brad Fitzpatrick's LiveJournal had database servers that could not keep up and web servers with…

In 2003 Brad Fitzpatrick's LiveJournal had database servers that could not keep up and web servers with memory to spare. He wrote memcached, a program that turned the spare memory of many machines into one large hash table, and gave it away; within a few years most large websites ran it. Its simplicity moved the hard part into the application, a difficulty usually put in a line attributed to Phil Karlton: there are only two hard things in computer science, cache invalidation and naming things. A decade later Rajesh Nishtala and colleagues described how far the idea had been pushed in "Scaling Memcache at Facebook" (2013): billions of requests a second, invalidation by delete, and a mechanism called a lease to stop both stale writes and stampedes. Their paper reacted to the failures that appear only at that size, which are the two in this chapter.

⚠The traps
  • The cache as source of truth: the sign is data written to the cache and nowhere else, or a decision such as a charge made from a cached value. A restart or an eviction loses it, or the decision is made on stale facts.
  • No expiry: the sign is a put without a time to live. One missed invalidation leaves a wrong answer in place until the next restart.
  • Stampede on expiry: the sign is a database load graph with regular spikes at the cache's time to live. Every request for a popular key recomputes it at once.
  • Caching to hide a slow query: the sign is a cache added because one query takes seconds. Every miss and every cold start is still that slow, and the first busy morning after a deploy finds it.
  • A personalised response under a shared key: the sign is a cache key that names the page but not the customer, for a value that includes something about the customer. One person's details are served to everyone.
  • The cold cache at deploy: the sign is a cache held in each server's memory, or flushed on release. The database receives full load at the moment the fleet restarts.
◉Spot it

The cache plan for the product page: "Key: product-page:{sku}. Value: the rendered page, comprising name, description, photograph keys, list price, the signed-in customer's trade discount and their 'you last bought this on…' line. Time to live: five minutes with jitter. Deleted when Catalogue or Promotions publishes a change to the product. Loads are single-flight. Checkout re-reads price and stock from the database."

Show the answer

Answer The value contains one customer's discount and purchase history, and the key names only the product. The sign is a personalised field in a value stored under a shared key: the first customer to load the page fixes what everyone sees for five minutes, including their trade price. The fix is to cache the shared part under the product key and fetch the personal part separately, per customer, or not cache it at all.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What is the hit ratio, and what load reaches the database if the cache is empty?
  2. For each cached item, how stale may it be, and what removes it when the truth changes?
  3. Which decisions, such as the price charged or the stock sold, are made from cached data?

Still argued: whether a system should depend on its cache. Rajesh Nishtala and colleagues (2013) describe a site that cannot run without one: the cache is the main read path, the databases are sized on that assumption, and engineering effort goes into keeping the cache correct and warm. Marc Brooker's "Caches, Modes, and Unstable Systems" (2021) argues that such a system has two modes, warm and cold, that it cannot climb out of the cold one under load because the database was never sized for it, and that a safe cache needs feedback, such as back pressure and limited concurrency, so that an empty cache does not pass the whole load through. The first position buys an order of magnitude in cost. The second buys a system that restarts.

What Ana learned

  • Give every cache entry both an expiry and an invalidation, and protect popular keys with single-flight.
  • Size the database for the load it receives when the cache is cold, or have a rehearsed way to warm it.
  • Read anything that decides money or stock from the system of record.

…but

The database is quiet at 2,000 pages a second. The network is not. Each page is still 1 MB, nearly all of it photographs, styles and scripts sent from London: the 16 Gbit a second that chapter 2 circled, on a connection that carries ten. And a trial customer in Toronto reports that the photographs take three seconds to appear.

Chapter 10 · Act IIICloser to the Customer#

The problem

Chapter 2's sheet had a circled line: 2,000 pages a second at 1 MB each is 16 Gbit a second, and Bramble's connection carries ten. The cache of chapter 9 made the pages cheap to build. It did nothing about sending them.

Ana asks why every page is a full megabyte every time, when most visitors have seen the logo and the stylesheet before. Kofi remembers why: a decision from last spring. A stylesheet change had gone out, browsers had kept the old stylesheet for a day as instructed, and customers saw the new page layout with the old styles: buttons over text, a checkout nobody could use. Priya's fix then was to tell browsers never to keep anything. Every visit has downloaded everything since.

Then there is Toronto. Lena has started a trial with a Canadian stationery blogger, and the first customers report three seconds of grey boxes where the photographs should be. A page needs about forty files. Each is requested from London, 80 milliseconds away and back, after an encrypted connection that takes several round trips to set up.

Priya's proposal is a second 10 Gbit line. Kofi's objection is that it puts more lorries on the same road: it does nothing for Toronto, and it pays twice to send the same photograph of the same planner to people who already have it.

The idea

Two questions decide how much traffic a site sends: may this response be reused, and how far away is the nearest copy?

Reuse is declared by the server. Every HTTP response can carry a Cache-Control header saying who may keep it and for how long. max-age gives a lifetime in seconds. public allows shared caches to keep it; private restricts it to the one browser; no-store forbids keeping it at all. A response may also carry an ETag, a fingerprint of its content. When a cached copy's lifetime runs out, the browser makes a conditional request: "I have the version with this fingerprint; has it changed?" If not, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body. That saves the bytes, though not the round trip.

The stylesheet problem is solved by naming. With versioned asset URLs, a file's name includes a fingerprint of its content: shop.8d1e07.css, planner.4f9a2c.jpg. A given URL can never change its content, so it may be cached for a year. A new stylesheet has a new name, the page refers to the new name, and no browser has an old copy under it. The mismatch of last spring becomes impossible, and nothing ever needs to be purged.

Response Header Why
Photographs, styles, scripts with versioned names Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable The content of this URL cannot change
A product page, the same for every visitor Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60, with an ETag Shared caches may reuse it for a minute
Basket, account, checkout Cache-Control: private, no-store One customer's data, never shared

The rule is to give static files a version in the name and a year's lifetime. It cannot apply to URLs you do not control the name of, the page itself or a link in an old email, and those take a short lifetime and an ETag instead.

Distance is solved by someone else's buildings. A content delivery network is corner shops near the customers, stocked from the depot. The provider runs caching servers in hundreds of cities: the edge. Bramble's own servers are the origin. A customer's request goes to the nearest edge, which answers from its cache if it can and otherwise fetches from the origin once, keeps the response as the headers allow, and serves the next thousand customers itself.

The arithmetic changes completely. The 950 KB of files per page never reaches London after the first request for each. What is left for the origin is page HTML at 50 KB, and with product pages reusable for sixty seconds, only the misses. Even with no page caching at all it would be 2,000 × 50 KB: 100 MB a second, under one gigabit. The second line is not needed. Toronto's forty files now come from Toronto.

The edge is also a reverse proxy: a server that accepts the customer's connection on the origin's behalf and makes its own request onward. That lets it do TLS termination, completing the encrypted handshake a few milliseconds from the customer and reusing a few long-lived connections to London, so the several round trips of connection set-up are short ones. Chapter 3's layer 7 load balancer is a reverse proxy too; this is the same idea, placed in every city.

How does a customer reach the nearest edge? Through DNS, the directory that says which depot serves your town. A browser asks for the address of Bramble's name, and with geographic routing the answer depends on where the question came from. DNS answers are themselves cached, for the time to live on the record, by resolvers Bramble does not control. A change to a record is seen only as old answers expire, so a record's time to live is how long a mistake, or a move, takes to reach everyone. Keep it short on records you may need to change in a hurry, at the cost of more lookups; lengthen it where nothing moves.

One last door. If the origin still answers anyone who finds its address, the edge can be bypassed, by a flood or by a scraper. Bramble's load balancers now accept connections only from the network's edge servers.

Remember it as: stock corner shops near the customers, give every file a name that changes when it does, and send only what nobody has seen.

◷How we got hereIn 1995 Tim Berners-Lee, whose office at MIT was along the corridor from Tom Leighton's, challenged…

In 1995 Tim Berners-Lee, whose office at MIT was along the corridor from Tom Leighton's, challenged colleagues to find a better way to deliver content than every reader converging on one server. Leighton and his student Danny Lewin answered with the mathematics of chapter 7, consistent hashing across a changing set of caches, and in 1998 founded Akamai, which began commercial service the following year. The protocol was ready for it: HTTP/1.1, standardised in 1997 and revised in 1999, had introduced the Cache-Control header and entity tags precisely so that browsers and intermediaries could reuse responses safely. Both were reactions to the same event, the "flash crowd", in which a page became popular and its single server became unreachable at exactly the moment the most people wanted it. Bramble met one in chapter 1.

⚠The traps
  • Uncacheable by default: the sign is no-store, or no caching header at all, on files that are identical for every visitor. Every visit downloads everything and the origin's bandwidth scales with traffic.
  • Purging instead of versioning: the sign is a release step that calls the network's purge function for files whose names did not change. The edge is cleared and the browsers are not, so customers see new pages with old styles.
  • Private pages cached at the edge: the sign is public, or a missing private, on a response that contains one customer's data. The next visitor to that URL is served someone else's account.
  • The long DNS time to live before a move: the sign is a record with a lifetime of a day on a name that is about to change address. For that day, part of the world is still sent to the old place.
  • The unprotected origin: the sign is an origin address that answers requests from anywhere. Attackers and crawlers skip the edge and its protection, and reach the servers the edge was sparing.
◉Spot it

A release note: "Styles and scripts are served through the content delivery network at /static/shop.css and /static/shop.js with Cache-Control: public, max-age=86400. On each release the deploy script uploads the new files and then purges /static/* at the edge. Product pages are public, s-maxage=60; basket and account pages are private, no-store. The origin accepts connections only from the edge."

Show the answer

Answer The file names never change, so the release relies on a purge. The sign is a fixed name with a day's lifetime and a purge step: the purge empties the edge but cannot reach browsers, which keep the old stylesheet for up to a day and apply it to new pages. The fix is to put a content fingerprint in each file name, cache it for a year, and delete the purge step.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which responses reach the origin at peak, and how many gigabits a second is that?
  2. When a file changes, how does a browser holding the old one come to fetch the new one?
  3. Can the origin be reached without passing through the edge?

Still argued: how much should happen at the edge. Kenton Varda's announcement of Cloudflare Workers (2017) argues that the edge should be programmable: the customer's own code runs in the edge servers, decides what is cached and where requests go, and can answer some requests without contacting the origin at all. Jerome Saltzer, David Reed and David Clark's "End-to-End Arguments in System Design" (1984) argues that functions belong at the endpoints that understand them, and that a function placed in the middle cannot be made complete or correct without their help. The first position gains speed for whatever can be computed without the database. The second notes that the data is still in one place, and that code far from its data waits on the same round trips it meant to avoid.

What Ana learned

  • Put a fingerprint in the name of every static file and let it be cached for a year.
  • Decide for each kind of response whether it is public, private or never stored, and write the header down.
  • Shorten a DNS record's lifetime days before the address behind it must change.

…but

The sale opens on a Monday at 09:00 and the pages fly. Orders arrive at twenty a second. Fulfilment's label worker, which turns each paid order into a courier label, manages eight. By ten o'clock the queue between Ordering and Fulfilment holds forty thousand orders and is still growing.

Chapter 11 · Act IIIThe Yard Was Full#

The problem

Monday, sale day, 09:00. Ordering takes orders at twenty a second and publishes each to a queue. On the other side one Fulfilment worker takes each order, asks the courier for a label and sends it to the warehouse printer, at eight a second. Twelve more arrive every second than leave: 43,200 an hour.

Nobody notices. The broker accepts everything it is given, its processor is idle, and every dashboard is green. At eleven the warehouse manager telephones to ask why orders placed at five past nine still have no label.

Priya starts four more workers. Five workers pull forty orders a second, and the courier's label service, which permits twenty-five requests a second, begins to answer slowly and then to refuse. Calls that took 100 milliseconds take a minute. The broker, having heard nothing about a message for thirty seconds, assumes its worker has died and hands the message to another. By noon some six hundred parcels have two labels each, and the courier charges for both.

Ana lists what went wrong. The queue hid a shortfall for two hours. Adding workers moved the bottleneck to somebody else's system. And a message delivered twice did its work twice. The Atlas mentioned backpressure in a paragraph of its chapter 14; this is the mechanism.

The idea

A queue is the waiting yard, and a worker is one of the loaders who clear it. A producer puts a message in and carries on; a consumer takes it out when it is ready. The two no longer need to run at the same speed, or even at the same time.

That makes load levelling possible: lorries arrive in a rush and are loaded at a steady pace. Workers need not match the peak. They need to beat the average, and the yard absorbs the difference at the price of delay. Bramble's peak is 20 orders a second for two hours, falling to about 5 afterwards, and the courier collects at four in the afternoon:

Workers Leaving per second Yard at 11:00 Yard empty by
1 8 86,400 19:00, after the courier has gone
2 16 28,800 11:44
3 24 0 never forms

Two workers would meet the courier: the yard grows by four a second through the peak and drains at eleven a second after it. Bramble runs three, because with two an order waits over twenty minutes for its label. That is the first rule of queues. A queue smooths a burst; it does not add capacity. Over any long stretch, more must leave than arrive, or the yard only grows.

Several workers on one queue are competing consumers: each message goes to exactly one of them, so adding workers raises the rate. It raises it until the next bottleneck, which here is the courier at 25 a second, so three workers at 24 is the ceiling and a fourth buys nothing. It also means messages are no longer handled in order.

Watching the yard. Two measurements matter. Queue depth is how many messages are waiting. Consumer lag is how old the oldest one is, and it is the better alarm, because it is stated in the terms the business cares about: a label within fifteen minutes. Monday's failure was a lag of over an hour that no dashboard showed.

Closing the gate. An unbounded queue accepts work for ever and reports nothing, until memory, disk or patience runs out. A bounded queue has a limit, and when it is reached the producer is told: its publish blocks or is refused. That signal is backpressure: closing the gate when the yard is full, and telling the road. It is only useful if it reaches something able to slow down. A batch import can pause. A web request can be answered "try again shortly". A paid order cannot be refused, so for the labels queue the limit is set high, the alarm fires long before it, and Ordering holds unsent messages in its outbox (the Atlas, chapter 15) meanwhile. Always bound the queue. The honest exception is work that must never be turned away, and it costs exactly this: a limit sized as an alarm, and somewhere durable for the producer to wait.

Taking a message is a loan. When a worker takes a message the broker hides it from the others for a visibility timeout. If the worker acknowledges in time, the message is deleted. If it does not, because it crashed or because it was slow, the message becomes visible again and is redelivered to someone else. So every message is delivered at least once and occasionally twice. Making the work safe to repeat is the Atlas's subject: the idempotent consumer and the dead-letter queue in its chapter 15, idempotency keys in its chapter 14. One thing belongs here: set the timeout longer than the slowest honest attempt.

Two more kinds of yard. A delayed message stays invisible until a set time: "release this stock reservation in fifteen minutes unless it has been paid for". The same mechanism runs scheduled jobs. And a priority queue lets urgent work overtake: the simplest form is separate queues with their own workers, so that a million marketing emails cannot stand in front of an order confirmation.

Remember it as: a yard lets lorries arrive in a rush and leave steadily, but only if more leave than arrive and someone is watching.

◷How we got hereMessage queues were enterprise plumbing long before the web: IBM's MQSeries, from 1993, moved messages…

Message queues were enterprise plumbing long before the web: IBM's MQSeries, from 1993, moved messages reliably between mainframes and everything else. The vocabulary came in 2003, when Gregor Hohpe and Bobby Woolf's Enterprise Integration Patterns gave names to sixty-five messaging designs, among them Competing Consumers: several receivers on one channel, so that work is shared and the rate rises with their number. The pattern reacted to consumers that processed one message at a time while the channel behind them filled. Queues became a rented utility when Amazon put its Simple Queue Service, in beta since 2004, into production in 2006, with the visibility timeout as its way of surviving a worker's death. What the patterns book did not dwell on, and operators learned afterwards, was the yard with no fence: a queue that never refuses is an outage postponed.

⚠The traps
  • The unbounded queue: the sign is a queue with no maximum length and a producer that has never had a publish refused. Overload is invisible until memory or disk runs out, and then everything fails at once.
  • The queue as database: the sign is code that inspects the queue to answer a question, or messages kept for days as the only record of something. Queues are for work in transit; they cannot be queried, and a purge loses the business's data.
  • The invisible slow consumer: the sign is monitoring of the broker's processor and disk with no alarm on depth or on the age of the oldest message. The queue grows for hours while every dashboard is green.
  • Work that cannot be repeated: the sign is a consumer that charges, prints or sends with no way to recognise a message it has seen before. Redelivery, which is normal, does the work twice.
◉Spot it

Billing's invoice queue: "Billing publishes each invoice request to a queue bounded at 100,000 messages; when the queue is full the publish fails and Billing retries from its outbox. Two competing workers render about four invoices a second each. Rendering is idempotent, keyed by invoice id. The visibility timeout is two minutes, longer than the slowest render. A message that fails five times goes to the dead-letter queue. We monitor the broker's processor, memory and disk, and whether each worker process is running."

Show the answer

Answer Nothing watches the queue itself. The sign is a monitoring list with the broker's health and the workers' existence, and no depth or lag: if the workers slow down, or arrivals pass eight a second, the queue fills quietly until it hits the bound and Billing starts failing. The fix is an alarm on the age of the oldest message, set from how late an invoice may be.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. At peak, what is the arrival rate, what is the service rate, and when is the queue empty again?
  2. What happens when the queue is full, and who is told?
  3. How old is the oldest message now, and at what age is somebody paged?

Still argued: whether a queue is a remedy for overload at all. Fred Hébert's essay "Queues Don't Fix Overload" (2014) argues that a queue in front of a slow component only delays the failure and hides it, and that the real constraint remains wherever it was. The honest designs, he says, are to push back on the sender or to drop work at the edge. Alex Homer and colleagues, in Microsoft's Cloud Design Patterns (2014), present queue-based load levelling as a standard remedy. A buffer between a task and the service it calls smooths intermittent heavy load, keeps the service available and lets it be sized for the average instead of the peak. They agree once numbers are attached. If the long-run arrival rate is below the service rate, the queue levels; if it is above, the queue is where the failure waits.

What Ana learned

  • Compare arrival rate with service rate before adding a queue, and work out when it empties after the peak.
  • Give every queue a bound, an alarm on the age of its oldest message, and a decision about who is told when it is full.
  • Size workers to the slowest thing downstream of them, and make every consumer safe to run twice.

…but

The sale's second day is calm, and Lena has an idea for its last. She wants every product page to say "3 left" and count down as people buy. Priya's sketch has each browser asking for the number once a second. And the only place that hears about each sale is a queue, which hands every message to one reader and then forgets it.

Chapter 12 · Act IIIThree Left#

The problem

Lena wants the last day of the sale to feel like a shop with a crowd in it: every product page showing "3 left", and the number falling while you watch.

Priya's sketch has each open page asking the server for the stock figure once a second. Ana does the arithmetic from chapter 2. At the sale peak 2,000 pages are opened a second, and a visitor keeps a page open for about a minute, so 120,000 pages are open at once. Each asking once a second is 120,000 requests a second: sixty times the load of the product pages themselves, for a number that changes, for most products, a few times an hour.

The second problem is where the number comes from. Every sale is announced as a message on a queue, and chapter 11's queue hands each message to exactly one worker. If the new counter service takes a message, Fulfilment never sees it. Priya adds a second queue and publishes everything twice. Then the search team wants the same messages, to hide sold-out products. Then Lena wants a live sales board. On Wednesday the board's service is deployed and needs to know what was sold on Monday and Tuesday, and those messages were deleted the moment they were handled.

Kofi says the yard was the right tool for work to be done once. This is something else: facts that many readers want, at their own pace, including readers who do not exist yet.

The idea

The log is the goods-in book kept for ever. It is an append-only sequence of records: new ones are added at the end and nothing is changed or removed by being read. Every record has a position, its offset, and each reader keeps its own bookmark saying how far it has got. Readers do not affect each other. One can be an hour behind while another is current, and a reader that did not exist on Monday can start at offset zero on Wednesday.

Retention is set by time or size, not by consumption: Bramble keeps seven days. And replay is ordinary: a reader with a bug is fixed, its bookmark is moved back, and it reads the same records again.

A log is partitioned for the reasons in chapter 7. Records with the same key, here the sku, go to the same partition and stay in order; there is no order between partitions. A consumer group is a team sharing one bookmark: its members divide the partitions among themselves, so a group scales like competing consumers, while separate groups each see every record.

Queue Log
A message goes to One consumer Every consumer group
After it is read Deleted Kept until retention expires
Order Lost across competing consumers Kept within a partition
A message that fails Retried alone, or set aside Blocks its partition until handled
Suits Tasks: do this once Facts: this happened

Labels stay on the queue; stock changes move to the log.

Batch and stream. With the facts in a log there are two ways to compute from them. Batch processing is the nightly stocktake: take a bounded set of records, say yesterday's, and process the lot. It is simple and can be rerun, and its answer is hours old. Stream processing is the running tally: handle each record as it arrives and keep the answer current. It gives results in seconds and has to cope with what batch never sees: records arriving late or out of order, and state that must survive a restart. Since a stream never ends, totals are taken over a window: orders in each minute, or units sold in the last fifteen. Lena's daily sales report is a batch. "3 left" is a stream. Use a stream when the answer is worth less every second it is late; otherwise a batch does the same sum with a fraction of the machinery.

Processing twice. A log reader can crash after doing its work and before saving its bookmark. On restart it reads the same records again. Delivery is at least once, as it was for queues, and exactly-once delivery cannot be built. What can be built is effectively-once processing: a result that is the same however many times a record is handled. A stock event does not say "one fewer"; it says "the planner now has 3 left, change number 5,117". Applying it twice changes nothing.

Telling the browser. Four ways, in rising order of machinery:

Who speaks Connection Suits
Polling Browser asks every few seconds A new request each time Updates that can be seconds late; cacheable at the edge
Long polling Browser asks; server answers when there is news Held open, then reopened Prompt updates where nothing newer is available
Server-sent events Server, down one long response One, kept open, reconnects by itself A feed from server to browser
WebSocket Either side One, kept open, its own protocol Conversation in both directions: chat, games

The counter only ever flows one way, so Bramble uses server-sent events: the push servers hold 120,000 idle connections, which an event-driven server manages easily, and send a few bytes when a number changes. It is the counter display that changes without anyone asking.

Fan-out. One sale of the planner must reach everyone watching the planner. Fan-out on write does the work when the fact arrives: push to every open connection for that sku. Fan-out on read stores the latest figure once and lets each viewer fetch it when they look. Writing is cheap when few are watching and ruinous when thirty thousand are: every sale becomes thirty thousand messages. So the push is coalesced to one update per product per second, however many sales occurred.

Remember it as: a yard gives each job to one loader and forgets it; the goods-in book is kept, and every reader has a bookmark.

◷How we got hereIn 2004 Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat described MapReduce, which let an ordinary programmer run a batch…

In 2004 Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat described MapReduce, which let an ordinary programmer run a batch job across thousands of machines. At LinkedIn, Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao found the batches too slow and the alternative, a bespoke pipeline between every pair of systems, unmanageable. In 2011 they published Kafka: a partitioned log that any number of systems could read at their own pace. Kreps's 2013 essay "The Log" argued that the log is the idea underneath databases, replication and stream processing alike. In 2014, in "Questioning the Lambda Architecture", he challenged the then-standard advice to run every computation twice, once as a slow correct batch and once as a fast approximate stream: if the log can be replayed, he argued, one stream processor can do both.

⚠The traps
  • Polling everything: the sign is a timer in the page that requests a value every second from the origin. Load is set by how many pages are open, not by how often anything changes.
  • Exactly-once assumed: the sign is a consumer that adds, increments or sends for each record, with its bookmark saved in a separate step. A crash between the two repeats the work and the total is wrong for ever.
  • The fan-out storm: the sign is one event producing a message per follower or viewer, with no limit on either. The most popular item generates more traffic than the rest of the system together.
  • A stream where a batch would do: the sign is a streaming pipeline feeding a report read once a day. The team operates state, windows and late data to produce a figure a nightly query would give.
◉Spot it

The live sales board: "A consumer in its own group reads order events from the log, partitioned by order id and kept for seven days. For each record it adds the order's total to a running figure in the board's database, and then saves its offset to the log. If the consumer crashes it restarts from its last saved offset. The board shows the running figure."

Show the answer

Answer The total is updated and the offset is saved in two separate steps. The sign is "adds" followed by "then saves its offset": a crash between them replays those records on restart and adds their totals a second time, so the board overstates sales. The fix is to make the step repeatable: record each order id with its total and sum distinct orders, or store the offset in the same database transaction as the figure.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Who else needs these messages, and can a reader added next month see what was sent before it existed?
  2. If this consumer handles the same record twice, is the result still right?
  3. How many clients hold a connection open, and how many messages does one change send?

Still argued: whether exactly-once is real. Tyler Treat's "You Cannot Have Exactly-Once Delivery" (2015) argues from the impossibility results of distributed computing that a message is delivered at most once or at least once, and that anything claiming otherwise has moved the problem into the consumer. The name, he says, misleads engineers into writing consumers that are unsafe. Neha Narkhede's "Exactly-Once Semantics Are Possible: Here's How Kafka Does It" (2017) describes idempotent producers and transactions that write a consumer's output and its offset atomically. The observable result is exactly once, she argues, and that is what users meant all along. The mechanism is not in dispute. The dispute is over the name, and over what happens at the edge of the transaction, where the effect is an email or a card payment and cannot be rolled back.

What Ana learned

  • Put facts that several systems need on a log, keep tasks on a queue, and say which is which.
  • Make every record safe to process twice, by carrying the new value or an identifier, before trusting any total.
  • Choose polling through the edge, server-sent events or a WebSocket by which side speaks and how late an update may be.

…but

The sale ends as the best week Bramble has had. Lena's next slide says North America, from January, with a second set of servers in Virginia so that Toronto is not eighty milliseconds from everything. In the first test the link between London and Virginia is cut for four minutes. Both sides keep selling, from what each believes is the stock.

Chapter 13 · Act IVWhich Copy Is Right?#

The problem

Bramble opens in North America in January, with app servers and a copy of every database in Virginia. The copies are followers: every write still crosses the Atlantic to the leader in London, 80 milliseconds there and back. A checkout makes several writes, and from Toronto it feels slow.

Priya's fix is the natural one. Make Virginia a leader too. Each region accepts writes from its own customers and sends them to the other in the background, so everybody's writes are local.

Kofi tests it by cutting the link between the regions for four minutes. Both sides keep trading. When the link returns there are forty boxes of a fine black pen in the warehouse, and London has sold thirty-one of them while Virginia has sold twenty-two. Fifty-three sold, forty to ship. A customer who changed her delivery address through one region and her telephone number through the other has lost one of the two, and nothing recorded which.

Nothing malfunctioned. Ana's question, when two copies of a record disagree, which copy is right, turns out to have no general answer. It has to be decided in advance, separately for each kind of data, and the deciding has a theory.

The idea

Start with where the depot picture breaks, because the break is the subject. Physical stock cannot be in two places: forty pens are forty pens. A record saying "forty pens" can be in London and in Virginia at once, and each copy can be reduced separately. Nothing in a copied number prevents both sides subtracting from the same forty. Only a rule about who may write prevents it.

A network partition is the road between two depots being closed, so that each must decide whether to keep trading. Partitions are rare and they are not optional. What a system does during one is a choice, and the CAP theorem states the limit of that choice. As proved, it says this: in an asynchronous network, one with no shared clock and where messages may be lost, it is impossible to implement a read/write data object that guarantees both availability, meaning "every request received by a non-failing node in the system must result in a response", and atomic consistency, meaning the object behaves as if it were on a single node, answering one operation at a time.

During a partition, each operation on shared data must either be refused on one side, which keeps it consistent, or be answered on both sides from what each has, which keeps it available and lets the copies diverge. The theorem says nothing about a healthy network, nothing about speed, and nothing that makes "consistent, available, partition-tolerant: pick two" a menu. The choice exists only while the road is closed, and it can be made differently per operation.

Daniel Abadi's PACELC adds the half that matters every day: if there is a partition, a system trades availability against consistency; else, when all is well, it trades latency against consistency. Toronto's slow checkout was that second trade. A write that must be confirmed by London costs 80 ms whether or not anything is broken.

"Consistency" here names a scale, and three points on it are worth knowing.

  • Linearizability: everyone reads the one book at head office. Each operation appears to take effect at a single instant between its start and its finish, so once a write has completed, every later read sees it. This is the C in CAP.
  • Causal consistency: operations that depend on one another are seen by everyone in the same order, so a reply never appears before its question. Unrelated operations may be seen in different orders.
  • Eventual consistency: the copies agree once the vans have done their rounds. If writes stop, all copies converge. It promises nothing about what a read returns meanwhile.

Two of these words are each used for two things.

Term Belongs to Promise
Consistency in ACID Transactions (chapter 6) A transaction leaves the data obeying its rules
Consistency in CAP Replicas The copies behave as one copy
Serializable Transactions over many records The result is as if they ran one at a time, in some order
Linearizable One operation on one record The result respects real time: completed writes are visible to all

A database can offer either of the last two without the other.

Quorums are how a system without a leader approaches consistency. Keep N copies. A write succeeds when W copies confirm it; a read asks R copies and takes the newest. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set: enough signatures from enough depots that any two decisions must share a signatory. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2, one copy may be unreachable and work continues. Choosing R and W per request is tunable consistency: W = 1 is fast and may be lost; R = 1 is fast and may be stale. The overlap is weaker than it sounds. The paper that popularised it says only that R + W > N "yields a quorum-like system", and with concurrent writes and nodes standing in for failed ones it is not linearizable.

When copies have diverged, something must reconcile them. Last write wins keeps the version with the later timestamp and throws the other away, silently; chapter 15 shows how arbitrary "later" is. Siblings keeps both versions and hands them to the application, which merges them: a basket becomes the union of both baskets.

Bramble decides per operation.

Browsing and baskets choose availability and low latency: they are served locally, may be seconds stale, and merge without harm. Stock and payment choose consistency: one leader, in London, and during a partition Virginia can fill baskets and cannot check out. North America is a tenth of orders, 5,000 a day, so a four-minute partition delays about fourteen orders. That is the price, and it is cheaper than thirteen pens that do not exist. The answer changes when North America has a warehouse of its own, or passes half of all orders: stock held there would have its leader there, and no record would have two writers.

Remember it as: when the road between depots closes, decide for each kind of entry whether to stop writing or reconcile later, and decide before it closes.

◷How we got hereThe definition came first: in 1990 Maurice Herlihy and Jeannette Wing defined linearizability, for objects…

The definition came first: in 1990 Maurice Herlihy and Jeannette Wing defined linearizability, for objects shared between processors, as the illusion that each operation takes effect at one instant. In 2000 Eric Brewer, who had built a search engine on clusters of cheap machines, told a conference that the systems of the day were promising strong consistency and constant availability across networks that could not be relied on, and conjectured that no system could keep both when the network split. Gilbert and Lynch proved it in 2002. Amazon's Dynamo paper of 2007 showed a production store built to stay writable, with quorums and sibling versions, and Werner Vogels's "Eventually Consistent" (2008) explained the bargain to practitioners. Abadi's PACELC, in 2010, reacted to CAP's silence about the normal case: with no partition anywhere, systems still give up consistency, and what they buy with it is speed.

⚠The traps
  • "We chose CA": the sign is a design for several machines that claims consistency and availability and says partitions will not happen. The network decides whether there is a partition; the design only decides what breaks.
  • One consistency level for everything: the sign is a single setting, strong or eventual, applied to every table. Either baskets are refused during a partition for no reason, or stock is sold twice.
  • Eventual consistency with no convergence story: the sign is "it will be consistent eventually" with no statement of what reconciles diverged copies. The copies stay different, and nobody finds out which is right.
  • Silent last write wins: the sign is conflict resolution by timestamp on whole records, with nothing logged. One of two valid changes disappears and no error is raised anywhere.
◉Spot it

A design note for customer profiles: "A profile holds a delivery address, a telephone number and a marketing preference. It may be edited in either region, so that the account page keeps working during a partition. Each region sends its changes to the other asynchronously. Where the same profile has been changed on both sides, the version with the later timestamp replaces the other. Checkout re-reads the address from London before dispatch."

Show the answer

Answer Conflicts are resolved by replacing the whole profile with the later version. The sign is "the version with the later timestamp replaces the other" on a record with independent fields: an address changed in one region and a telephone number changed in the other are both valid, and one is discarded without a trace. The fix is to merge field by field, each field carrying its own version, or to keep both versions and ask the customer.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. When the link between sites is cut, which operations are refused and which carry on with stale data?
  2. For each write, how many copies must confirm before the customer is told it succeeded?
  3. When two copies hold different values for one record, what decides the result, and is anything discarded?

Still argued: whether giving up consistency for availability is a good trade. Werner Vogels (2008) argues that at very large scale failures are continuous, and that a system which refuses writes during them fails its customers. Most business operations, he adds, tolerate a short inconsistency if it is designed for. Michael Stonebraker's "Errors in Database Systems, Eventual Consistency, and the CAP Theorem" (2010) argues that partitions are a small share of real failures beside software faults and operator mistakes, and that eventual consistency helps with none of those. Surrendering consistency to survive the rarest failure is, on his account, a poor exchange. Brewer's own retrospective of 2012 moved toward the middle: the choice arises only during a partition and can be made operation by operation.

What Ana learned

  • Sort operations into those that may be stale and those that may be refused, and write the list down before adding a second site.
  • Give every piece of data one place where it is written, unless it merges harmlessly.
  • Ask of any eventually consistent store what makes the copies agree again, and what is thrown away when they do.

…but

So stock has one leader, in London, and everything depends on there being exactly one. In February the machine running that leader freezes for forty seconds. The failover manager promotes the follower. Then the old leader wakes, unaware that anything has happened, and carries on accepting orders.

Chapter 14 · Act IVTwo Head Offices#

The problem

At 14:11 on a Tuesday in February the virtual machine running the stock leader in London stops. It has not crashed. The host underneath it is being moved, and for forty seconds the machine executes nothing at all.

The failover manager does its job. Thirty seconds without a heartbeat means the leader is dead, so it promotes the follower in Zone B and begins repointing the app servers.

At second forty the old leader resumes. From its point of view no time has passed. It still believes it is the leader, and it is configured to carry on alone if its follower stops answering. Three app servers still hold connections to it, and it accepts their writes. For ninety seconds, until someone notices, Bramble has two leaders. Eleven orders are recorded on a machine whose changes go nowhere, and two of them are for stock the new leader has already sold.

This is the split brain that chapter 5 named and postponed. Priya's first fix is to raise the timeout to two minutes, so that a forty-second pause is survived. Kofi points out the two costs: every real failure now closes the shop for two minutes, and nothing limits a pause to forty seconds. Her second idea is a second manager to watch the first. Ana asks who decides when the two managers disagree, and nobody answers.

The idea

Every node proves it is alive by sending a heartbeat every second or so, and failure detection is noticing silence. The trouble is that silence has three causes. The node is dead, or it is paused, or the network between you and it is broken. From outside they look the same. A timeout is therefore a guess, and a design that is only correct when the guess is right is not correct.

Two mechanisms make the guess safe to get wrong. One ensures that only one new leader can be chosen. The other ensures that an old leader, whatever it believes, cannot do damage.

Choosing one leader: majority. Let the decision be made by a fixed set of voters, and require more than half to agree. Any two majorities of the same set share at least one voter, and a voter votes once per round, so two different leaders cannot both be chosen. It is chapter 13's overlapping signatures, applied to an election. Three voters survive the loss of one; five survive two. On the losing side of a partition no majority exists, so no leader is elected there and that side stops: consistent, not available.

Use an odd number of voters, in at least three failure domains. Four voters tolerate one loss, as three do, at the cost of another machine. Two is the worst number: a majority of two is two, so when either is lost, or the link between them, the survivor cannot tell whether it is the majority, and must either stop or risk a split brain.

Consensus is the general problem: the depot managers agreeing, by majority, on one head office. More exactly, it is getting several machines to agree on a value, such as who leads or what the next entry in a log is, so that a decision once made is never unmade, though machines crash and messages are lost. Paxos is the classic algorithm. Raft is the one written to be understood, and it has three parts. Leader election: time is divided into numbered terms, and at most one leader can be elected in a given term. Log replication: the leader appends each change to its log and counts it committed when a majority hold it. Safety: an entry once committed appears in the log of every later leader. Such systems keep working while a majority of the servers are running and can reach one another.

Nobody at Bramble should write this. A coordination service (etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul are the usual ones) is a small store that runs consensus among three or five voters and offers the results as simple operations: elect a leader, hold a lease, keep a little configuration. Bramble's database failover is rebuilt on one, with voters in Zone A, Zone B and a third zone that holds a vote and no data.

Stopping the old leader: leases and fencing. Leadership is granted as a lease: an appointment that expires unless renewed. A leader that cannot renew must stop. But the paused machine of 14:11 did not know its lease had expired; it woke and wrote. A lease limits how long two leaders can believe they lead. It does not stop the stale one acting.

That takes a fencing token: the numbered key issued with each appointment; the lock refuses an older number. Each time the coordination service grants leadership it issues a number larger than any before. Every write carries the writer's token, and the store that receives writes remembers the highest it has seen and refuses anything lower.

public final class FencedStockRepository implements StockRepository {
    private final Map<Sku, StockLevel> stock = new HashMap<>();
    private long highestTokenSeen = 0;        // stored with the data in a real system

    /** Every write names the fencing token issued with the writer's lease. */
    @Override
    public synchronized void save(StockLevel level, long fencingToken) {
        if (fencingToken < highestTokenSeen) {
            throw new StaleLeaderException(
                    "token " + fencingToken + " is older than " + highestTokenSeen);
        }
        highestTokenSeen = fencingToken;
        stock.put(level.sku(), level);
    }
}

Notice where the check is. The coordination service cannot protect the store; only the store can refuse a write. That is the limit of every distributed lock. Inside one process a lock is absolute. Across machines, the holder can be paused beyond the lock's expiry and resume in the middle of its work, so the lock is a strong hint and the token is the guarantee. A lock without one is adequate for avoiding duplicated effort, and inadequate where a second writer would corrupt something.

With both mechanisms the split brain is resolved: the majority rule means only one side can appoint a leader, and the token means the other side's late writes are refused.

Remember it as: a majority appoints one head office and numbers the appointment, and the lock refuses any key carrying an older number.

◷How we got hereLeslie Lamport's "The Part-Time Parliament", published in 1998, proved that a majority of unreliable machines…

Leslie Lamport's "The Part-Time Parliament", published in 1998, proved that a majority of unreliable machines can agree safely, and told it as the story of a Greek island's legislature, which is partly why few readers understood it. Google built on it anyway. Mike Burrows's 2006 paper on Chubby, a lock service, explained the design choice that shaped the field: put consensus in one small service so that other systems use it and do not implement it. Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout published Raft in 2014 with understandability as its stated goal, reacting to the difficulty engineers had in implementing Paxos correctly, and the newer open-source coordination services adopted it. Martin Kleppmann's 2016 essay "How to do distributed locking" supplied the last piece for practitioners: a lease can always expire under a paused holder, so the resource itself must check a fencing token.

⚠The traps
  • Home-made consensus: the sign is leader election written in application code, with a table of heartbeats and a "who is alive" query. It works until the first pause or partition, and then elects two.
  • A lock without a fencing token: the sign is a distributed lock with an expiry, and writes that carry nothing the store can check. A holder paused past the expiry writes after someone else has taken over.
  • A timeout taken as proof of death: the sign is a failover that acts on silence and does nothing to stop the old leader. A node that was merely slow returns as a second leader.
  • The two-node cluster: the sign is two voters, or two sites with no third. When the link fails neither side has a majority, and the system either stops or splits.
◉Spot it

Billing's nightly invoice run: "Two schedulers stand ready, and only one must run the job. Each tries to take a lock in the coordination service, with a thirty-second lease that the holder renews every ten seconds while it works. The holder allocates invoice numbers and writes the invoices to Billing's database. If the holder dies, its lease expires and the other scheduler takes the lock and carries on. The coordination service has three voters in three zones."

Show the answer

Answer The writes to Billing's database carry nothing that identifies which grant of the lock they were made under. The sign is a lease with an expiry and a store that accepts writes from anyone who believes they hold it: a scheduler paused for a minute wakes, finishes its batch and allocates invoice numbers the other scheduler has already used. The fix is to take the fencing token issued with the lock and have the database refuse writes with an older one.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. How many voters are there, where are they, and how many can be lost before no leader can be chosen?
  2. If the old leader was only paused and wakes up, what refuses its next write?
  3. Which component decides that a node is dead, and what happens when it is wrong?

Still argued: whether a lock service built on a cache is safe. Martin Kleppmann (2016) argues that the Redlock algorithm, which takes a lock on several independent cache servers, depends on assumptions about clocks and pauses that real systems break, so it cannot guarantee that only one client acts. Correctness, he argues, needs a consensus system and a fencing token. Salvatore Sanfilippo, the algorithm's author, replied (2016) that its timing assumptions are modest and hold in practice, and that a client can detect most long pauses by checking the time after acquiring. A store able to check a fencing token, he added, could have prevented the conflict by itself, making the lock unnecessary. Both agree that a single cache server is enough when the lock only prevents wasted work. They differ on whether "holds in practice" is good enough when the lock protects data.

What Ana learned

  • Let a consensus-backed coordination service with an odd number of voters in three places choose the leader, and write none of it yourself.
  • Treat every timeout as a guess, and make the design safe for the case where the node was only slow.
  • Make the store that receives writes check a fencing token, because only it can refuse a stale leader.

…but

There is one leader now, provably. A week later support escalates an order whose cancellation is timestamped a second before the order was placed, and a customer whose change of address was accepted and then vanished. Both involved two servers writing in the same moment. In both, the later clock won, and the later clock was wrong.

Chapter 15 · Act IVWhat Time Is It?#

The problem

Support has two cases that make no sense.

The first is order 49206518. The customer placed it and cancelled it a second later, having ordered the wrong size. The record says it was cancelled at 10:15:01 and placed at 10:15:02. The nightly reconciliation job, which sorts events by timestamp, found a cancellation for an order that did not yet exist, ignored it, and the wrong size was shipped.

The second is a change of address. The customer typed "12 Mill Lane", saw the mistake, and corrected it to "14" a second later. The profile says 12. Profiles are merged field by field, as chapter 13's exercise advised, and within a field the later timestamp wins. Here the later write lost.

Ana finds the cause in an afternoon. The two requests in each case were handled by different servers. One server's clock was two seconds fast; a synchronisation job had been failing quietly for a month. So the earlier event carried the later time.

Priya's fix is to repair the job and add an alarm, and that is worth doing. Kofi's point is that it changes the size of the problem and not its nature. Synchronised clocks agree to within some milliseconds on a good day and drift apart when anything is wrong. Two events closer together than the error cannot be put in order by reading clocks, and the two events that matter are always close together.

The idea

A computer has two kinds of clock, and most bugs with time come from using the wrong one.

Wall clock Monotonic clock
Tells you The date and time Time elapsed since some arbitrary start
Adjusted Yes: synchronised over the network, and may jump forwards or back Never jumps back
Comparable between machines Only roughly Not at all
Use for Showing a time to a person Timeouts, durations, rate limiters

The wall clock is the clock on each depot's wall, all slightly different. The difference between two machines' wall clocks is clock skew, and it is never zero. The monotonic clock is a stopwatch: useless for saying when, exact for saying how long.

So wall-clock timestamps from different machines cannot settle which of two close events came first. This is what goes wrong when they are asked to:

Last write wins is therefore a way of losing data. With skewed clocks the wrong write wins. With perfect clocks, of two writes made at the same moment, one is still thrown away and nobody is told. It is acceptable only for values where a lost concurrent update does no harm, such as "last seen at".

The alternative is to stop asking what time it was and ask what could have caused what. A logical clock is numbering the entries instead of timing them. In the simplest, the Lamport timestamp, every node keeps a counter. It adds one for each event, sends the counter with every message, and on receiving a message sets its own counter to one more than the larger of the two. The guarantee is one-directional: if event a could have influenced event b, then a's number is lower than b's. The converse does not hold. A lower number does not mean "happened first"; the two events may be concurrent, with no connection between them. Breaking ties by node name gives a total order that everyone agrees on, and Lamport's own paper calls that order somewhat arbitrary. It is enough for the first case: carried on each message, the counter puts a cancellation after the order it refers to.

A vector clock keeps one counter per node and carries the whole set. Comparing two of them gives three possible answers: this one came before, that one came before, or neither, which means they were concurrent. That third answer is what last write wins hides. It is how a store knows it holds siblings, in chapter 13's sense, and must merge them instead of choosing.

A CRDT, a conflict-free replicated data type, is a data structure designed so that concurrent changes always merge to the same result on every copy, with no coordination: a counter, a set, a basket that takes the union. And TrueTime is the opposite bet, made by Google's Spanner: put atomic clocks and satellite receivers in every data centre, have the clock report an interval that is certain to contain the true time, and make each transaction wait out the uncertainty, a few milliseconds, before it commits. Then a transaction that commits before another starts always has the earlier timestamp. It works, with special hardware and a wait on every write.

Time has one more job, which is naming things. A unique identifier is a docket number no two depots can issue twice.

Scheme Made by Good Bad
Auto-increment One database's counter Short, in order One issuer: a bottleneck, and impossible across partitions or regions
Random, 128 bits Any machine No coordination at all Unordered, so inserts land all over the index of chapter 4
Time-ordered, 128 bits Any machine: a timestamp, then random bits No coordination; new rows arrive in roughly sorted order Reveals when it was made
Snowflake-style, 64 bits Any machine with a unique number: timestamp, machine number, sequence Fits one integer; roughly sorted Machine numbers must be handed out; a clock stepping back must be handled

The Atlas wrote OrderId.next() and never said what was inside. This is what Bramble puts there:

public final class OrderIdGenerator {
    private static final long EPOCH = 1_704_067_200_000L;    // 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z in milliseconds
    private final long machineId;                             // 0 to 1,023, unique per running process
    private long lastMillis = -1;
    private long sequence = 0;                                // 0 to 4,095 within one millisecond

    public OrderIdGenerator(long machineId) { this.machineId = machineId; }

    public synchronized OrderId next(long wallClockMillis) {
        if (wallClockMillis < lastMillis) {                   // the wall clock has stepped back
            throw new IllegalStateException("clock moved back; refusing to issue identifiers");
        }
        if (wallClockMillis == lastMillis) {
            if (sequence == 0xFFF) throw new IllegalStateException("4,096 issued this millisecond");
            sequence++;
        } else {
            sequence = 0;
            lastMillis = wallClockMillis;
        }
        return new OrderId(((wallClockMillis - EPOCH) << 22) | (machineId << 12) | sequence);
    }
}

Forty-one bits of time, ten of machine, twelve of sequence. The machine numbers come from chapter 14's coordination service. The identifiers sort roughly by creation, which keeps the index compact, but "roughly" is the word: they order rows for storage, and they do not say which of two orders was really first.

Remember it as: every depot's wall clock is slightly wrong, so number the entries instead of timing them, and never let a clock decide whose write survives.

◷How we got hereLeslie Lamport's 1978 paper "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System" began as a…

Leslie Lamport's 1978 paper "Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System" began as a reaction to a proposal for keeping database copies in step using timestamps. He saw, with special relativity in mind, that there is no universal "now" between machines, only what could have caused what, and that a simple counter captures it. Later the large websites needed identifiers without a central database: Twitter announced Snowflake in 2010, sixty-four bits of timestamp, worker number and sequence, generated anywhere. Marc Shapiro and colleagues defined conflict-free replicated data types in 2011, making merge a property of the data. And in 2012 James Corbett and his co-authors at Google described Spanner, which turned back to physical time and made it trustworthy with hardware, by admitting its error and waiting it out.

⚠The traps
  • Ordering by wall clock: the sign is a comparison of timestamps that were taken on different machines, in a sort, a merge or a conflict rule. Skew reverses events that happened close together.
  • The auto-increment identifier across partitions: the sign is a database sequence used as the key of data that is, or will be, written in more than one place. Either one database issues every identifier, or two issue the same one.
  • A timestamp as a unique identifier: the sign is a key built from the time to the millisecond. Two events in the same millisecond collide, and a clock stepping back repeats old keys.
  • Trusting the client's clock: the sign is a time sent by a browser or a phone and used to order, expire or validate. The device's clock is whatever its owner has set it to.
◉Spot it

Returns: "Each return request is given an identifier made of the warehouse code and the time of the request to the millisecond, for example LDS-20270214T101500123. It is generated on whichever app server receives the request; the servers' clocks are synchronised and monitored. The identifier is the primary key of the returns table and is printed on the label. A request that times out is retried with the same identifier."

Show the answer

Answer The identifier is a timestamp and nothing else. The sign is a key whose only varying part is the time: two returns at the same warehouse in the same millisecond, on one server or two, receive the same key, and one insert fails or overwrites the other. The fix is to add a machine number and a sequence, as above, or to use a time-ordered identifier with random bits.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Where does the design compare timestamps taken on two different machines, and what happens if one clock is two seconds wrong?
  2. Which clock measures each timeout and duration: the wall clock or the monotonic one?
  3. Who issues identifiers, and what prevents two issuers from producing the same one?

Still argued: whether a system may rely on synchronised clocks for correctness. James Corbett and colleagues (2012) show that it may, if the clock's error is measured and exposed: with a bound of a few milliseconds and a deliberate wait, a database spanning continents gives transactions a true global order, which logical clocks alone cannot. Justin Sheehy's "There Is No Now" (2015) argues that almost nobody has such clocks, that ordinary synchronisation fails silently and without bound, and that designs should rest on causality and explicit conflict handling, with physical time as a hint. The first is a statement about what is possible with the right hardware. The second is a statement about what is prudent without it.

What Ana learned

  • Never order events from different machines by wall-clock time; carry a counter or a version instead.
  • Use the monotonic clock for every timeout and duration, and the wall clock only to show people a time.
  • Generate identifiers on any machine from time, a machine number and a sequence, and treat their order as approximate.

…but

The clocks are distrusted and the identifiers sort. Then Lena has news: the illustrator has said yes. Kofi books a rehearsal for the drop at a tenth of its size, and it is over in four minutes: one script and a wave of retries, arriving together, flatten checkout.

Chapter 16 · Act VThe Doorman#

The problem

The drop is 10,000 numbered notebooks by an illustrator with four million followers, on sale at 09:00 on a Friday in May. Marketing expects half a million people in the first minute.

Kofi's rehearsal runs at one-tenth scale on a Tuesday night, with a test product and rented load generators. It fails in three ways in four minutes.

First, one generator, playing a scalper's script, sends 400 add-to-basket requests a second from a single account. Bramble has a limit, which Priya added in the spring: 50 requests a second per account, counted on each app server. There are twelve servers, so its real allowance is 600, and all 400 pass.

Second, checkout slows, and the shop's own page code does what it was written to do: retry after one second, then two, then four. Every browser that failed in the same second retries in the same second. The servers begin to recover, are hit by the returning wave, fall over, and are hit by the next, which is larger.

Third, the servers treat everything alike. Requests for recommendations, for the live stock counter, and from a search engine's crawler queue beside payments, and all of them time out together.

The Atlas gave rate limiting and load shedding a paragraph in its chapter 14. The drop needs the mechanisms.

The idea

Three defences, from the outside in: limit each client, protect the service whoever is asking, and make clients behave.

Rate limiting is the doorman's allowance per haulier: a cap on what one client may ask, so that a script spends its own allowance and nobody else's. Four algorithms are in use.

Algorithm How it counts Bursts Catch
Token bucket Tokens drip into a jar at a steady rate, up to a capacity; each request spends one Allowed, up to the capacity Two numbers to choose
Leaky bucket Requests join a short queue that drains at a fixed rate; overflow is refused Smoothed away A burst waits instead of passing
Fixed window A counter per calendar minute Twice the limit across a boundary The boundary
Sliding window A count over the last sixty seconds Not beyond the limit More to store

The token bucket is the usual choice, because real clients are bursty and it says plainly how bursty they may be.

public final class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;            // the largest burst allowed
    private final double refillPerNano;     // the steady rate
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefill;

    public TokenBucket(long capacity, double tokensPerSecond, long nowNanos) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = tokensPerSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.tokens = capacity;
        this.lastRefill = nowNanos;
    }
    /** True if the request may pass; false means answer 429 with a Retry-After. */
    public synchronized boolean tryAcquire(long nowNanos) {
