        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (nowNanos - lastRefill) * refillPerNano);
        lastRefill = nowNanos;
        if (tokens < 1.0) return false;
        tokens -= 1.0;
        return true;
    }
}

The algorithm is the small part. Where the limit is enforced decides whether it works. The count must be one count: held at the edge, or in a store every server shares, never in each server's memory. And it must come first. A limiter that runs after the request has been authenticated, parsed and looked up in the database has already spent what it was meant to save. Enforce per-client limits at the edge, before the origin sees the request. A limit that needs to know something only the service knows, such as a seller's plan, has to sit in the service, and costs a lookup per request.

Load shedding protects the service from the total, whoever is sending it. It is turning lorries away at the gate before the yard jams. Chapter 1's table says a saturated server serves everyone badly; a server that refuses the excess in a millisecond serves the rest well. Admission control is the decision at the door: count the requests in flight, and when the count passes what the service can finish in time, refuse new ones at once. Refusal must have an order. Bramble's is payments and checkout first, then browsing, then recommendations and the live counter, then crawlers. Shedding the last two classes is graceful degradation: serving the essentials and closing the gift-wrap counter. The page still sells notebooks; it stops suggesting pens.

Clients must behave, including Bramble's own. A failed call should be retried only if it is safe to repeat, which the Atlas's chapter 14 covers under idempotency keys, and then with three rules. Exponential backoff: wait longer after each failure, so a struggling service gets room. Jitter: randomise each wait, because backoff alone keeps clients that failed together in step; choosing a random wait between zero and the backoff ceiling spreads the returning wave flat. And a retry budget: retries may be at most a set share of traffic, say a tenth, because three layers each making three attempts turn one failure into twenty-seven requests.

One client-side technique adds load on purpose. A hedged request attacks tail latency: if a read has not answered by the time 95 in a hundred usually have, send a second copy to another server and take whichever returns first. It costs about 5% more requests and cuts the p99 sharply. It is only for reads that are safe to run twice, and it must stop when the service is busy, or it is a retry storm with a better name.

For the drop none of this is enough alone. Half a million arrivals in a minute is 8,300 a second, four times the largest load Bramble has served, and only 10,000 of those people can succeed. A virtual waiting room is numbered tickets and a car park outside the estate. Visitors are held on a static page served from the edge, each is given a place in line, and they are admitted at the rate checkout has been tested to serve: 100 a second, five times the sale's peak. Everyone else sees an honest position and then an honest "sold out". The waiting room is not for ordinary days. It is one more component in front of everything, and it earns that position only when arrivals are known to exceed capacity.

Remember it as: give every haulier an allowance at the gate, turn lorries away before the yard jams, and tell them not to all come back at once.

◷How we got hereThe bucket algorithms come from telecommunications networks: Jonathan Turner described the leaky bucket in…

The bucket algorithms come from telecommunications networks: Jonathan Turner described the leaky bucket in 1986 as a way to police how fast a subscriber could send into a shared network. Web services needed the same policing two decades later, when they began to be called by programs. Michael Nygard's Release It! (2007) set down what production had taught him: that a system must defend itself against its callers and its dependencies, fail fast when it cannot do the work, and never trust the other side to behave. The client's half was put most clearly by Marc Brooker in "Exponential Backoff and Jitter" (2015), which showed by simulation that clients backing off in step collide again and again, and that randomising the wait cuts both the total work and the time to finish. Each was reacting to outages that the system's own retries had prolonged.

⚠The traps
  • The per-server rate limit: the sign is a limit held in each server's memory behind a load balancer. The real allowance is the limit times the number of servers, and it grows when the fleet scales up under attack.
  • Retries without jitter: the sign is a retry delay that is a constant or a pure power of two. Clients that failed together return together, and the load arrives in waves.
  • Limiting after the expensive work: the sign is a limiter that runs after authentication, parsing or a database read. Refused requests cost nearly as much as accepted ones.
  • Shedding without priorities: the sign is an overload policy that drops requests at random, or oldest first, whatever they are. Payments are refused while recommendations are served.
  • Hedging a request that is not idempotent: the sign is a duplicate request sent for speed on a call that creates or charges. The fast path does the work twice.
◉Spot it

The limiter in front of the checkout service: "Each of the twelve app servers keeps a token bucket per account in its own memory: capacity 20, refilled at 5 a second. A request that finds no token is answered 429 with a Retry-After header. The limiter runs before any database work. Clients back off exponentially with jitter and keep to a retry budget of 10%."

Show the answer

Answer The buckets live in each server's memory. The sign is "each of the twelve app servers keeps": the load balancer spreads one account's requests over all twelve, so the account's true allowance is a burst of 240 and 60 a second, and it rises whenever servers are added. The fix is one bucket per account, held at the edge or in a store all the servers share.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. If one client sends ten times its allowance, what does it receive, and which component says no?
  2. When the service is saturated, which requests are refused first, and how much work has been spent on them by then?
  3. After a failed call, how long does the client wait, how is the wait randomised, and what caps its retries?

Still argued: whether limits should be fixed numbers or found automatically. Paul Tarjan's account of rate limiting at Stripe (2017) describes fixed limits per customer, with a few load shedders behind them; the case for explicit numbers is that they are predictable, can be explained to the customer who hits them, and can be reasoned about in an incident. Eran Landau and colleagues at Netflix (2018) argue that any fixed limit is wrong the day after it is set, because capacity changes with every deploy, and describe servers that discover their own concurrency limit continuously from measured latency, as network congestion control does. The first gives up some capacity for clarity. The second gives up clarity for capacity.

What Ana learned

  • Keep one count per client, at the edge, and check it before doing any other work.
  • Decide the order in which requests are refused before the day they must be.
  • Give every client backoff, jitter and a retry budget, starting with the shop's own pages.

…but

The second rehearsal passes: the crowd waits outside, the script gets its allowance and no more, and checkout takes a steady hundred a second. Kofi asks what nobody has asked. All of it runs in London. There is a document, written in March, for moving the shop to Virginia if London is lost, and nobody has ever followed it.

Chapter 17 · Act VThe Day the Region Went Dark#

The problem

Wednesday, 23:00, ten weeks before the drop. Kofi blocks every network path into and out of London, as if the region had vanished, and starts a stopwatch. The document from March says Virginia will be serving customers within thirty minutes.

The first step is to open the document. It is on the wiki, and the wiki runs in London. Kofi has a printout.

Step two works: the copy of the orders database in Virginia is promoted to leader by hand, with London cut off at the edge so that nothing can reach the old one. It was replicating asynchronously and was six seconds behind. At the evening rate of an order and a half a second, nine orders that customers saw confirmed do not exist in Virginia.

Step three is to grow Virginia from the two app servers that serve North America to twelve. New servers fetch the application from the image registry. The registry is in London. So is the pipeline that could publish the image somewhere else. Priya finds a copy on a laptop.

Step four, changing the DNS records, works in five minutes, because chapter 10 shortened their lifetime.

Virginia is serving at 02:40: three hours and forty minutes. On Thursday Kofi tries the last line of the document, restoring the orders database from backup. It takes nine hours, and the backup from the second of June will not open at all.

Nothing was wrong with any single component. The plan needed the place it was a plan for losing.

The idea

A failure domain is everything that floods together. A machine is one. So is an availability zone, a building with its own power, cooling and network, and a region, a town with several such buildings some kilometres apart. So, less obviously, is anything shared: one configuration service, one registry, one deploy that goes everywhere at once. Blast radius is how much stops when a domain fails. The design work is to put copies in different domains and then hunt for whatever still joins them.

Zones and regions buy different things. Zones are a millisecond or two apart, close enough for the synchronous replication of chapter 5, so losing a zone need lose no data. Regions are far apart, 80 ms for Bramble, so replication between them is asynchronous and the standby is always a little behind. That gap has a name, and so does the stopwatch.

Recovery point objective Recovery time objective
Picture How many pages of the book you can afford to lose How long the doors may stay shut
Measured in Seconds of data Minutes of outage
Set by Replication lag; how often backups are taken Detecting, deciding, switching, warming up
Bramble's rehearsal 6 seconds: 9 orders 3 hours 40 minutes
Bramble's target 10 seconds 15 minutes

Both are business decisions with a price. Lena accepts ten seconds of orders at risk, since the payment provider's records allow them to be rebuilt, and will not accept an afternoon closed.

Read it as chapter 3 taught: look for what stands alone. The registry box exists once, and Virginia has one zone and a sixth of the servers.

There are two shapes for a second region.

Active-passive Active-active
Picture A standby depot kept warm Two depots both trading
Normal day One region serves; the other receives copies Both serve, and both accept writes
When a region is lost Failover: promote, redirect, scale up The survivor carries on
Hard part The standby is rarely exercised Two writers: every conflict of chapter 13
Cost Capacity that idles Complexity in every write path

Bramble is between the two: Virginia is active for reading and passive for writing. That is a legitimate place to stay. Full active-active is the right answer only for data that has a conflict design: each record with a single home region, or values that merge. Chapter 19 puts a figure on when it pays.

Wednesday's lessons become rules.

Nothing needed for recovery may live only in the region being recovered from. Registry, pipeline, secrets, documents and backups are copied to Virginia, and the printout stays in the drawer.

The standby must be able to take the load without asking anyone. Scaling up during a disaster depends on the things that are failing. Virginia's two servers already cover a normal peak of 150 pages a second; it stays that size and is raised by hand before an event. The same holds between zones: twelve servers across two zones leaves six if one is lost, good for 1,200 pages a second and short of a sale's 2,000. Priya doubles the floor to twelve per zone. The price is idle machines, which chapter 19 will question.

A backup is the copy in the fireproof safe, and a restore test is opening the safe to check you can read it. Replicas protect against losing a machine. Only a backup protects against a mistake, because a mistake is replicated. A backup that has never been restored is a hope. Bramble now restores one every month, to a different region, and times it.

Failover has a second half. Failback is returning home: London comes back holding nine orders Virginia never saw, must be reconciled, rebuilt as a follower and promoted at a quiet hour. It is rehearsed as well.

Two wider ideas. Data residency: the law in some places requires certain personal data to stay within a jurisdiction, which constrains where copies and backups may be put, so the question goes to a lawyer before the second region is chosen. And cells: instead of one large system per region, run several complete, independent copies, each a self-contained depot serving its own customers, so a fire stays in one building. A bad deploy or a runaway customer then harms one cell's share of customers. A cell-based architecture costs a routing layer and many of everything, and it suits platforms with hundreds of servers and customers who must be shielded from each other. Bramble has two dozen servers; its two regions are cells enough.

The second rehearsal, a week later, takes fourteen minutes.

Remember it as: know what floods together, keep the safe in another town, and open it before the fire.

◷How we got hereRecovery point and recovery time are terms from the disaster-recovery plans of the mainframe era, when the…

Recovery point and recovery time are terms from the disaster-recovery plans of the mainframe era, when the standby was a second data centre and the backup went there by road. Cloud providers made the standby rentable by the hour: Amazon introduced availability zones in 2008, and for a while a second zone seemed protection enough. Then, in April 2011, a storage failure in one zone crippled storage operations across a whole American region and took many well-known sites down for a day or more, and on Christmas Eve 2012 a failure in the same region's load balancers interrupted Netflix streaming on many devices. Netflix's answer, described by Ruslan Meshenberg and colleagues in 2013, was to serve from several regions at once and to practise evacuating one. It reacted to the discovery that a region is a failure domain too, and that an unpractised standby is no standby.

⚠The traps
  • Backups never restored: the sign is a backup job with a green tick and no record of a restore. The first restore happens in an emergency and finds the corrupt file, the missing key or the nine hours.
  • Failover never practised: the sign is a recovery document older than the last change to the system. The steps no longer match, and the time it promises was never measured.
  • Active-active without a conflict design: the sign is two regions accepting writes to the same records, and "the database replicates both ways" as the whole answer. The first partition produces divergent data and a silent winner.
  • The shared dependency across zones: the sign is one service, in one zone, that every zone calls: configuration, sessions, a registry. The redundancy on the diagram fails together.
  • A recovery plan that needs the failed region: the sign is a recovery step that fetches something, an image, a secret or the plan itself, from the place being recovered from. The plan cannot start.
◉Spot it

Ordering, drawn for a review of zone failure. The load balancers are one per zone, and the coordination service's voters are not shown.

Show the answer

Answer The session store exists only in Zone A and both zones depend on it. The sign is a node with no counterpart in the other failure domain and arrows into it from both: when Zone A fails, Zone B's servers are healthy and nobody can stay signed in. The fix is a replicated session store with a copy in each zone.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. If this region vanished now, how many seconds of confirmed orders would be lost, and how many minutes until customers are served?
  2. Which things needed during a failover exist only in the region being failed?
  3. When was a backup last restored, and how long did it take?

Still argued: whether a second region should be a standby or a peer. Ruslan Meshenberg and colleagues at Netflix (2013) argue for peers: a region that takes no traffic is never truly tested, its capacity is a guess, and failing over to it is a rare and frightening act, whereas shifting traffic between regions that are both live is routine. Martin Kleppmann (2017) describes multi-leader replication, which peers that accept writes require, as dangerous territory to be avoided where possible, because conflict handling is subtle, poorly supported by many databases and a rich source of lost data. The first argues from the failover that fails. The second argues from the writes that conflict.

What Ana learned

  • State the recovery point and recovery time as numbers the founder has agreed to, and measure both in a rehearsal.
  • Keep every tool the recovery needs, including the plan, outside the region it recovers.
  • Restore a backup on a schedule and practise failing back as well as failing over.

…but

Lena hears "fourteen minutes" and asks whether that is good. Nobody can answer. Bramble has never written down how much failure it is prepared to accept, so it has no way to say whether fourteen minutes is a triumph or a breach.

Chapter 18 · Act VPromises with Numbers#

The problem

"Is fourteen minutes good?" Lena's question about the failover has no answer, and the week supplies three more like it.

Priya was on call and was paged thirty-one times: a cache node's processor over 80%, a disk at 70%, a follower two seconds behind. None of the thirty-one touched a customer. On Thursday evening the payment provider slowed down and three checkouts in every hundred failed for forty minutes. Nobody was paged, because no alert watches whether checkouts succeed.

Then sales forwards a contract for signature. The office-supplies reseller, 8% of Bramble's orders, has been promised "99.99% availability" with refunds for any breach. Nobody in engineering was asked what Bramble achieves, because nobody in engineering knows.

Ana sees one gap behind all three. Bramble measures its machines in detail and has never stated, as a number, what its customers are owed. So it cannot say whether an outage was acceptable, whether a page was worth waking someone for, or whether a contract can be kept. The Atlas introduced service level objectives in a paragraph of its chapter 20. This chapter is how they are set and what they are for.

The idea

Three terms, routinely confused, and each built on the one before.

Service level indicator Service level objective Service level agreement
Picture What you measure at the gate The promise you publish The contract, with a penalty
Form Good events ÷ all events A target for the indicator over a window A looser target, and what is owed if it is missed
Bramble's checkout Successful checkouts ÷ attempts, counted at the load balancer 99.9% over 30 days 99.5% a month, to the reseller
Who it is for Engineers Engineering and the business Customers and lawyers

A service level indicator must be measured where the customer is, for chapter 1's reason, and it must count what the customer cares about: a checkout that returns an error page quickly is fast and bad. A service level objective turns it into a promise. A service level agreement is always looser than the objective behind it, so that the alarm rings before the lawyer does. The contract on Lena's desk has it backwards.

The objective is 99.9% and not 100% for a reason. A hundred percent is unreachable: the customer's own connection is less reliable than that. By a common rule of thumb, each added nine costs ten times the last. And a system that may never fail may never be changed. The gap is useful. It is called the error budget: the late deliveries you may still afford this quarter.

Bramble takes 1,500,000 orders in thirty days. At 99.9%, the budget is 1,500 failed checkouts, or about 43 minutes of complete outage. Now Lena's question has an answer. Fourteen minutes is a third of a month's budget: affordable twice in a month, not four times. Thursday's incident, 108 failed checkouts, spent about 7%.

A budget only matters if spending it has consequences, agreed beforehand. Bramble's error-budget policy is two sentences. While budget remains, teams release as they please and may spend it on purpose. When it is gone, releases stop, except fixes, until the thirty-day figure recovers. Both halves matter: the first is permission to take risks, and the second is the only thing that makes the objective more than a wish.

What to watch. For any service, four measurements cover most of what goes wrong, the golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Chapter 1 met three of them. They belong on the dashboard.

What to be woken for. Alert on symptoms, not causes. A symptom is the customer being hurt: checkouts failing, pages slow. A cause is a full disk or a busy processor, and there are hundreds, most of which hurt nobody on any given night. Causes belong on dashboards and in tickets. The rule gives way for a cause that is certain to become a symptom soon, such as a disk that will be full in four hours, and the price of the exception is a page that might have waited.

The symptom worth paging on is the budget being spent too fast. Burn rate is the speed of spending relative to the speed that would use exactly the whole budget in the window. At a burn rate of 1, the budget lasts thirty days. Thursday's 3% failure rate against a budgeted 0.1% was a burn rate of 30: at that pace the month's budget is gone in a day. Bramble pages when the rate has been above 14 for an hour, which is 2% of the month's budget gone, and opens a ticket when it has been above 1 for three days. Priya's thirty-one pages become none, and Thursday becomes one.

Testing the promise. An objective says what should happen when things fail. Chaos engineering is finding out, by causing failures deliberately and watching: stop a server, cut a link, slow a dependency, with a stated expectation, a limited blast radius and a way to stop. A game day is the same thing as a scheduled exercise for people as well as machines; chapter 17's rehearsal was one. It is the fire drill, and the error budget is what pays for it.

Learning from the breach. After an incident, a blameless postmortem records what happened, what it cost in budget, what made it hard to notice and what will change. Blameless is a method, not a courtesy. It assumes everyone acted sensibly on what they knew and asks what the system told them. People who expect blame stop reporting what they saw, and the next incident takes longer.

Remember it as: measure at the gate, publish a promise short of perfect, and spend the difference on purpose.

◷How we got hereService level agreements come from telephone and outsourcing contracts, where they were written by lawyers…

Service level agreements come from telephone and outsourcing contracts, where they were written by lawyers and measured monthly. The engineering version came from Google, whose site reliability teams, from 2003, faced a standing quarrel: developers were rewarded for shipping and operators for stability. Their answer, set out for everyone else in Site Reliability Engineering, edited by Betsy Beyer and colleagues in 2016, was to agree a target short of perfection and treat the remainder as a budget both sides spend, which turned an argument into arithmetic. Netflix supplied the other half. Having moved to rented machines that could vanish at any time, it described in 2010 a tool called Chaos Monkey that killed its own production servers at random, so that surviving the loss of one became routine instead of hoped for. It reacted to resilience that existed only on diagrams.

⚠The traps
  • An objective of one hundred percent: the sign is "zero downtime" as a target, or four nines chosen because it sounds right. There is no budget, so every change is a risk nobody may take, and the target is missed anyway.
  • An alert for every cause: the sign is a pager that fires on processor, memory and disk thresholds. People are woken for things that hurt no customer, and learn to ignore the pager.
  • An agreement without an objective: the sign is a contractual availability figure that engineering does not measure, or one stricter than the internal target. The first anyone hears of a breach is the refund.
  • Blame in the postmortem: the sign is a root cause that is a person's name, or "human error". The conditions that made the mistake easy are left in place for the next person.
  • No error-budget policy: the sign is an objective on a dashboard and no agreed consequence for missing it. Releases continue through the breach and the number becomes decoration.
◉Spot it

The checkout objective, as drafted: "Indicator: successful checkouts divided by attempts, counted at the load balancer. Objective: 99.9% over thirty days, a budget of 1,500 failures. Paging: burn rate above 14 for one hour. Ticket: burn rate above 1 for three days. Policy: when the budget is spent, releases stop except fixes. Contract with the reseller: 99.95% each month, with service credits."

Show the answer

Answer The contract promises more than the objective. The sign is an agreement stricter than the internal target: Bramble can meet 99.9%, raise no alarm, and still owe credits every month it lands between the two figures. The fix is a contract looser than the objective, such as 99.5%, or an objective raised above the contract, with the cost of that extra reliability agreed first.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What is the indicator, where is it measured, and what was its value over the last thirty days?
  2. How much error budget is left this month, and what changes when it reaches zero?
  3. Which alerts page a person, and does each one mean customers are being hurt now?

Still argued: how failure should be rehearsed. Yury Izrailevsky and Ariel Tseitlin's account of Netflix's "Simian Army" (2011) argues for continuous, random failure in production during working hours. Only production is real, only constant exposure keeps every team honest, and a weakness found on a Tuesday afternoon is cheaper than one found on a Sunday night. Kripa Krishnan's description of Google's disaster-recovery testing (2012) argues for planned exercises: scheduled, scoped, with a control room and the power to call them off. An uncontrolled test of a critical system, on this view, is simply an outage. Both insist the tests touch real systems. They differ on who should be surprised.

What Ana learned

  • State what customers are owed as a ratio with a target and a window, and measure it where they are.
  • Agree in advance what happens when the error budget runs out, and keep every contract looser than the objective.
  • Page people only when the budget is burning fast, and send everything else to a dashboard.

…but

A month on, every objective is met, and by a wide margin: checkout has run at 99.99% since the target was set. The same week finance sends the infrastructure bill. It was £60,000 a month before the sale and is £105,000 now. And Marcus has a proposal for the drop: three regions, all active.

Chapter 19 · Act VThe Bill#

The problem

Finance sends one line: infrastructure was £60,000 a month before the sale and is £105,000 now. Bramble takes 1,500,000 orders a month, as it did then. Each order used to cost four pence to serve. It now costs seven.

Nobody decided to spend the extra £45,000. Ana and Kofi spend a Friday afternoon finding it, line by line, and each line has a history. The app-server floor was doubled from 12 to 24 after chapter 17's rehearsal, so that either zone could carry a sale alone, and there is no sale; the fleet peaks at 2% busy. Each busy database gained three more followers in the fortnight before chapter 9's cache went in; with nineteen reads in twenty now answered by the cache, they idle. Six machines run a stream-processing cluster for the live sales board, which Lena opens twice a week. Three years of backups sit on the fastest storage there is. And £8,000 a month is for data leaving the provider: debug logs, uncompressed, shipped to an outside logging service.

Marcus's proposal arrives the same afternoon, and it is the opposite of a saving. For the drop, and for good, Bramble should run in three regions, all active, every write accepted wherever it lands. His estimate is £30,000 a month and two engineers.

The idea

Cost is the rent, paid on every depot whether or not lorries come. The first tool is a unit. A monthly total says nothing; cost per order, or per request, can be compared across months and attached to decisions. Four pence became seven with no change in what customers received, and a design review can now ask what a proposal adds to the figure.

The second tool is a rule for telling headroom from waste. Chapter 2's spare third and chapter 17's standby in Virginia are capacity that a number justifies: a peak, a recovery time. Waste is capacity whose number has gone. So Kofi's list has three columns: what load justified this, what that load is today, and who would notice if it went.

Item Justified by Today Decision Monthly
App servers: 24 A sale peak of 2,000 pages a second with a zone lost 150 at peak; 2% busy Back to 12, autoscaled; twelve per zone before events −£9,000
Three extra followers per database 10,000 queries a second, before the cache About 40 reach the database at a normal peak Remove −£12,000
Stream cluster for the sales board "Live" figures Read twice a week Nightly batch query −£7,000
Backups on fast storage Nobody chose it Never read Cold tier after 30 days −£3,000
Debug logs sent outside A week of debugging in August Still on Sample and compress −£8,000
Virginia at normal-peak capacity; cache; coordination voters Recovery time of 15 minutes In use Keep £6,000 stays

That is £39,000 removed: £66,000 a month, 4.4 pence an order. Priya removes the followers herself; she added them.

Over-provisioning versus autoscaling. A fleet fixed at the size of its worst day is idle on every other day. Autoscaling follows the daily cycle, and chapter 3's rule covers the rest: raise the floor by hand before a known event. The half that was forgotten is the other direction. Every temporary increase gets an end date when it is made.

Storage tiers and egress. Providers sell storage in tiers: fast and dear, slower and cheaper, and archival, which costs almost nothing to keep and a fee to read. Data should move down as it ages; chapter 7's old order partitions are candidates. Egress is the charge for bytes leaving: to the internet, to another region, to a third party. It appears on no architecture diagram, and any design that moves data across a boundary pays it for ever.

Managed versus self-run. A managed database or queue costs more per unit than the same software on your own machines, and comes with someone else's on-call. The usual rule is to rent the managed service until its bill exceeds the cost of people who could run it well. The rule bends for large, steady workloads, where owning can be much cheaper, and what it costs is those people's attention, which was otherwise going into the product.

Operational complexity as a cost. The stream cluster's invoice was £7,000. Its real cost included the two engineers who understood it, its upgrades and its pages. Every component carries that second bill, and it is why chapter 8 counted stores and chapter 17 counted regions. Simplicity is capacity too: the capacity to change things.

Scaling back down is therefore a practice with a date in the diary: each quarter, every component is asked for its number again.

Now Marcus. His case is the one Netflix made: a standby is never truly tested, so make every region live and failover disappears. Three numbers answer it. Bramble's objective is 99.9%, a budget of 43 minutes a month, and a rehearsed failover takes 14: the present design meets the promise. Fourteen dark minutes at half an order a second is 420 orders, about £10,000 at an average order of £24; twice a year, £20,000, against £360,000 a year for his design. And stock cannot be merged, as chapter 13 showed, so "every write accepted anywhere" would mean either consensus across continents on every checkout or the chance of selling the same notebook twice. For the drop itself, which lasts under two minutes, there is a cheaper protection: if London is unhealthy at 08:45, the drop moves to Saturday.

So: not yet. His design is right when a regional outage costs more than the design does, which at today's prices is about eighteen times Bramble's volume, or when the objective must be 99.99%, whose monthly budget of four minutes no failover fits inside.

Remember it as: rent is paid on every depot whether or not lorries come, so ask each depot, every quarter, which lorries it is for.

◷How we got hereIn 2015 Frank McSherry, Michael Isard and Derek Murray asked a rude question in "Scalability!

In 2015 Frank McSherry, Michael Isard and Derek Murray asked a rude question in "Scalability! But at what COST?": how many machines does a published scalable system need before it beats one competent program on a laptop? For several well-known systems the answer was hundreds of cores, or never. Oz Nova's essay "You Are Not Google" (2017, first published under the name Ozan Onay) made the same point about choosing technology: the famous designs solved problems of a size most companies will never have, and the first step is to check that you have the problem. In 2023 Marcin Kolny of Amazon's Prime Video described rebuilding a monitoring service from distributed, serverless parts into a single process, cutting its cost by 90%. Each reacted to scale pursued as a virtue instead of a cost.

⚠The traps
  • Résumé-driven scaling: the sign is a technology proposed with its famous users named and its required load unstated. The team acquires the operating burden of a large company without the problem that justified it.
  • Scaling for load that never came: the sign is a component sized from a forecast, running at a few percent busy a year later. The forecast was never revisited and the rent is paid monthly.
  • Ignoring egress: the sign is a design that copies data between regions, or out to another company, with no figure for bytes a month. The charge arrives after launch and scales with success.
  • Never scaling back: the sign is a capacity increase with a start date and no end date. Every event leaves the fleet a little larger, permanently.
◉Spot it

A change request: "For the November promotion, raise the app-server floor from 12 to 24 on the 20th. The figure comes from last year's peak times 1.5, at 70% busy. Extra cost: £9,000 a month. A load test at the new size is booked for the 18th. Owner: Priya. The increase is covered by the events budget."

Show the answer

Answer The request says when the increase starts and not when it ends. The sign is a temporary change with one date: in February the floor is still 24, and nobody remembers why. The fix is an end date in the same request, and an alert if the floor is still raised after it. The sizing, the test and the ownership are sound.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. What does this design add to the cost of one order, in pence?
  2. What measured load justified each component, and what is that load today?
  3. For each temporary increase in capacity, on what date does it end?

Still argued: what the Prime Video story proves. Marcin Kolny's account (2023) is that the distributed version hit a scaling limit at a twentieth of the expected load and cost far too much, because every step passed data through storage and an orchestrator, and that one process doing the same work removed both problems. He presents the distributed design as the wrong fit for this workload. Werner Vogels's reply, "Monoliths are not dinosaurs" (2023), is that running software teaches things about a workload that were not known when it was designed, and that no architecture fits every case. The lesson he draws is to revisit architecture as facts arrive, not to prefer one shape. They differ on whether its first design was a mistake or a stage.

What Ana learned

  • Track the cost of one order, and ask of every proposal what it adds to that figure.
  • Give every component a number that justifies it, and every temporary increase an end date.
  • Answer a proposal for more scale with what an outage costs, what the design costs, and the volume at which the two meet.

…but

The bill is back to 4.4 pence an order. The drop is nine days away: 10,000 notebooks, half a million people at 09:00, and so far a list of mechanisms that have never been drawn as one design. Lena wants to see it on Thursday. Marcus will be presenting his.

Chapter 20 · Act VThe Drop#

The problem

Thursday, eight days before the drop. Marcus presents first, and his slide is handsome: fourteen boxes. The 10,000 notebooks are split into sixteen partitions across two regions, so that no single record is hot. Purchase requests are appended to a log, and a stream processor allocates units from it. Reservations live in a new key-value store that accepts writes in either region. Both regions are active.

Lena asks one question: will it sell exactly 10,000? Marcus says the partitions reconcile within seconds, so eventually, yes.

Ana has no diagram. She has one page, and it starts with what must be true: each notebook is numbered, so 10,001 is not an apology, it is a second customer holding number 4,117. She asks for an hour at the whiteboard and says she will draw nothing for the first twenty minutes.

What Bramble has never done is use the previous nineteen chapters in order, starting from the requirement and ending with what it chose not to build. Kofi says that order is the method, and that the method matters more than any box.

The idea

A design is produced in eight steps, and the diagram is the fifth.

1. Requirements. What must be true, and what may give. Sell 10,000 numbered notebooks, one per customer, never 10,001. Tell each buyer within seconds whether they have one. Hold it for five minutes while they pay; release it if they do not. Keep the rest of the shop working. Serve people roughly in order of arrival. May give: a buyer in Toronto waits a little longer; nobody can reserve during a failover.

2. Estimates. Half a million arrivals in a minute is 8,300 a second, four times the sale peak. Only 10,000 can succeed, so 98% of arrivals need a cheap, honest "no". Checkout has been tested at 100 a second, five times the sale's 20, so the notebooks are reserved in about 100 seconds. One stock row takes 100 updates a second against a leader good for 5,000: 2%.

3. Interface. POST /drop/reservations returns a reservation and its expiry, or "sold out", or "slow down" with a time to retry. POST /orders pays for a reservation. GET /drop/status returns the number left. Both writes are idempotent; the Atlas's chapter 14 covers idempotency keys.

4. Data model. One stock row for the notebook. A reservations table: customer, expiry, state, unique per customer. Taking a reservation is chapter 6's conditional update and one insert, in one short transaction. This is a reservation with expiry: stock is decremented at once, and a delayed message from chapter 11 fires five minutes later and, if the reservation is still unpaid, marks it expired and adds one back.

5. High-level design. Now the boxes, each one from a chapter.

6. Deep dives. The stock row is a hot key on purpose: 100 short updates a second, with no network call inside the transaction, is well within one row's reach; it stops being so somewhere past a thousand. Once the count reaches zero, "sold out" is served from the edge, so the other 490,000 arrivals never touch London. The number left is polled through the edge, a second stale, because pushing to half a million browsers would be chapter 12's fan-out storm.

7. Failure modes. For each box, what customers see when it fails. The leader dies: chapter 14's election promotes the synchronous follower in about thirty seconds, no reservation is lost, and the waiting room keeps the crowd outside meanwhile. The payment provider slows: reservations simply hold, and Lena may extend the five minutes. The waiting room fails: the edge says "back shortly" and nothing behind it floods. London is unhealthy at 08:45: the drop moves to Saturday.

8. Trade-offs. Say what was given up. This design refuses reservations for thirty seconds if the leader fails, charges Toronto 80 ms a write, and depends on one region for one morning. In exchange it cannot oversell.

Then the review. Ana puts both designs through questions the team has asked before.

Question, and its chapter Ana's design Marcus's design
What is the peak rate in requests per second, and what multiple of the daily average is it? (2) 8,300 arriving, four times the sale peak; 100 admitted Not stated
Which resource saturates first as load rises, and at how many requests per second? (1) The stock row, past 1,000 a second Unknown: untested
What is the partition key, and which frequent queries do not include it? (7) No partitions "How many are left?" asks all sixteen; a buyer sent to an empty partition is refused while another has stock
When the link between sites is cut, which operations are refused and which carry on with stale data? (13) Virginia cannot reserve Both sides sell; the total may pass 10,000
If this consumer handles the same record twice, is the result still right? (12) Expiry is conditional on state The allocator must be made effectively-once
Who backs up, upgrades and is paged for the new store, and have they agreed? (8) No new store Nobody, with eight days left
What measured load justified each component, and what is that load today? (19) Each box has a line in step 2 Sixteen partitions for 100 writes a second

The decision is Ana's design, and Marcus agrees on the numbers. One thing of his is kept: every reservation is appended to the log, so the allocation can be audited afterwards. The decision is written up as a record, a practice the software architecture book covers.

Deliberately not built: partitioned stock, a second writing region, a new datastore, a stream allocator, cells.

What would change the decision: a need to reserve more than 1,000 units a second; drops of a million units; stock held in two regions for local delivery; an objective of 99.99%; North America passing half of orders.

Remember it as: requirements, numbers, interface, data, boxes, risks, failures, trade-offs, in that order, and write down what you chose not to build.

◷How we got hereDesign reviews are as old as engineering, but the material in this book was for decades spread across…

Design reviews are as old as engineering, but the material in this book was for decades spread across database textbooks, operating-systems papers and the folklore of a few large companies. Martin Kleppmann's Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2017) put it in one place, organised by the questions a designer faces instead of by product, and gave working engineers the vocabulary to argue from mechanisms. It reacted to a period in which systems were chosen by name. The eight steps have a humbler origin: technology companies began asking candidates to design a system on a whiteboard, and guides to that interview, such as Alex Xu's in 2020, settled on an order much like the first six. What interviews leave out is the last two steps, because nobody is paged for a whiteboard.

⚠The traps
  • Boxes before requirements: the sign is a design presented as a diagram, with no sentence saying what must be true. The boxes answer a question nobody has agreed on.
  • A design with no numbers: the sign is "a large spike" or "high traffic" where a rate should be. Nothing can be sized, and no alternative can be compared.
  • A single design with no alternative: the sign is a proposal with no section on what else was considered. The trade-offs are invisible because there is nothing to trade against.
  • Ignoring failure modes: the sign is a diagram in which every arrow works. The design is tested for the first time by the first failure.
  • Building for permanent peak: the sign is capacity sized for the one extreme hour and left in place. The drop lasts two minutes; the fleet returns to twelve at noon.
◉Spot it

A summary for the summer flash deals: "Requirement: each deal's stock is sold exactly once, and the rest of the shop stays up. The deals will bring a very large spike in traffic. Interface and data model as for the drop. Design: edge, waiting room, twenty-four app servers until the end of the day, one leader with a synchronous follower. If the leader fails, reservations pause for thirty seconds. Alternative considered: stock partitioned by region, rejected because one row suffices. Given up: local writes for Toronto."

Show the answer

Answer There is no estimate. The sign is "a very large spike" where step 2 should be: without an arrival rate nobody can say whether twenty-four servers, one row or the waiting room's admission rate are right, or check the claim that one row suffices. The fix is a peak rate in requests per second with its source.

✎At the whiteboard
  1. Which numbers is this design sized by, and where did each come from?
  2. Which alternative was considered, and at what measurement would it become the better design?
  3. For each component, what do customers see when it fails?

Still argued: how much to design before building. Malte Ubl's account of design documents at Google (2020) argues for writing the design down first, with its alternatives and trade-offs, because a wrong turn found in code costs far more than one found on paper, and because a document is reviewed by people who would never read the code. Martin Fowler's "Is Design Dead?" (2004) argues that designs fixed up front encode guesses about requirements that turn out wrong, that a design should start simple and be changed as facts arrive, and that the skill to cultivate is making change cheap. Ubl himself limits documents to problems that are genuinely ambiguous. Fowler himself allows a broad starting architecture, and wonders whether some things are too painful to add later. The disagreement is over where that line falls.

What Ana learned

  • Start every design from what must be true and a peak rate, and draw nothing until both are written.
  • Put every proposal, including your own, through the same questions, and keep one alternative on the page.
  • Record what was not built and the measurement that would change your mind.

…but

The drop opens at 09:00 on Friday. In the first minute 512,000 people arrive, and the notebooks are reserved in 104 seconds. Three hundred and twelve reservations expire unpaid and are offered again; by 09:09 all 10,000 are sold, none twice. There is no next crack, only the next drop. The method is on a card by Ana's desk, and the epilogue is that card, at length.

EpilogueThe Depot#

This is the card by Ana's desk, at length. Nothing here is new. It is arranged for the second reading, for the design review, and for the moment someone says a word in a meeting and you want to know what it is for and how it goes wrong.

The metaphor table

Every concept in the book has a place in one network of depots. If you can place a word here, you can usually explain it.

Concept Metaphor Chapter
Request / response A lorry arriving at the gate and leaving loaded 1
Latency / throughput How long one lorry waits / how many lorries leave per hour 1
Percentile / tail latency The slowest lorry in a hundred, which is the one that complains 1
Utilisation / saturation How full the loading bays are / the queue down the road when they are all full 1
Bottleneck The one narrow gate every lorry must pass 1
Scaling up / scaling out A bigger depot / more depots 1, 3
Stateless service A bay where any loader can serve any lorry, because nothing is kept at the bay 3
Load balancer / health check The dispatcher at the gate sending lorries to bays / the dispatcher's glance to see which bays are staffed 3
Single point of failure The only bridge into the estate 3
Index The aisle signs and the catalogue at the front desk 4
Full table scan Walking every aisle to find one box 4
Connection pool The fixed number of trolleys; a loader without one waits 4
Write-ahead log The goods-in book, written before anything is put on a shelf 4
Replication / leader / follower Copying the stock book to other depots / the head office book / the branch copies 5
Replication lag The copy that arrives on the evening van 5
Failover / split brain A branch becomes head office / two branches both believing they are 5, 14
Transaction / isolation One clerk's complete stock movement / how much one clerk sees of another's half-finished count 6
Lost update / write skew Two clerks each selling the last box / two clerks each checking the rota and both going home 6
Pessimistic / optimistic lock Roping off the aisle / checking the shelf label has not changed before you write 6
Partitioning / partition key Splitting stock across depots / the rule that says which depot holds which box 7
Hot key The one box everybody wants, in one depot 7
Consistent hashing Redrawing depot territories so that only a few streets change hands 7
Datastore choice Shelving, bins, cold room and barn: each built for one kind of goods 8
Search index The catalogue you can look up by any word on the label 8
Object storage The bulk barn: big things, fetched whole, by ticket 8
Cache / TTL / invalidation The shelf by the counter / the date after which you restock it / pulling an item off it when the aisle price changes 9
Cache stampede Every clerk running to the same aisle when the counter shelf empties 9
CDN / edge Corner shops near the customers, stocked from the depot 10
DNS The directory that says which depot serves your town 10
Queue / worker / load levelling The waiting yard / the loaders who clear it / lorries arrive in a rush and are loaded at a steady pace 11
Backpressure Closing the gate when the yard is full, and telling the road 11
The log / offset / consumer group The goods-in book kept for ever / each reader's bookmark in it / a team sharing one bookmark 12
Batch / stream The nightly stocktake / the running tally 12
Push to the browser The counter display that changes without anyone asking 12
Network partition The road between two depots is closed, and each must decide whether to keep trading 13
Linearizable / eventual consistency Everyone reads the one book at head office / the copies agree once the vans have done their rounds 13
Quorum Enough signatures from enough depots that any two decisions must share a signatory 13
Consensus / leader election The depot managers agreeing, by majority, on one head office 14
Fencing token The numbered key issued with each appointment; the lock refuses an older number 14
Lease An appointment that expires unless renewed 14
Wall clock / logical clock The clock on each depot's wall, all slightly different / numbering the entries instead of timing them 15
Unique identifier A docket number no two depots can issue twice 15
Rate limit / token bucket The doorman's allowance per haulier / tokens dropped in a jar at a steady rate, one spent per lorry 16
Load shedding / graceful degradation Turning lorries away at the gate before the yard jams / serving the essentials and closing the gift-wrap counter 16
Retry with jitter Coming back later, and not all at the same minute 16
Virtual waiting room Numbered tickets and a car park outside the estate 16
Failure domain / zone / region Everything that floods together / a building / a town 17
Active-passive / active-active A standby depot kept warm / two depots both trading 17
RPO / RTO How many pages of the book you can afford to lose / how long the doors may stay shut 17
Backup / restore test The copy in the fireproof safe / opening the safe to check you can read it 17
Cell A self-contained depot serving its own customers, so a fire stays in one building 17
SLI / SLO / error budget What you measure at the gate / the promise you publish / the late deliveries you may still afford this quarter 18
Chaos engineering / game day The fire drill 18
Cost The rent, paid on every depot whether or not lorries come 19

One warning travels with the table: a box of stock is in one depot or another, and a record can be in three at once, slightly out of date in two. Chapters 5 and 13 are about that difference.

The diagram legend

Colour means the same thing in every diagram. A solid arrow is a request that waits for its answer; a dashed arrow is a transfer nobody waits for; a box around nodes is a failure domain, labelled as a zone or a region; a store takes writes unless it is drawn as a copy.

The review checklist

Every trap from every chapter, with the sign a reviewer would notice. Read down the section that matches the design in front of you.

Measuring and scaling (chapters 1–3)

  • Averages that hide the tail (ch. 1, The Morning the Shop Went Viral): a dashboard whose only latency tile is a mean, measured on the server.
  • Scaling out before measuring (ch. 1, The Morning the Shop Went Viral): a proposal to add servers that does not name the saturated resource.
  • Running hot (ch. 1, The Morning the Shop Went Viral): a resource at 85% or more on a normal peak, described as efficient.
  • Coordinated omission (ch. 1, The Morning the Shop Went Viral): a load test whose generator waits for each reply before sending the next request.
  • Designing for the average day (ch. 2, The Back of the Envelope): a capacity figure obtained by dividing a daily total by the seconds in a day and stopping there.
  • False precision (ch. 2, The Back of the Envelope): an estimate of 57.87 requests per second built on a peak factor somebody guessed.
  • Load testing with unrealistic data (ch. 2, The Back of the Envelope): a test that requests one product, as one user, against an empty database.
  • No headroom (ch. 2, The Back of the Envelope): a plan in which estimated peak equals measured capacity.
  • Sticky sessions as state (ch. 3, Two of Everything): a balancer configured to pin each customer to one server so that their session survives.
  • The health check that lies (ch. 3, Two of Everything): a health endpoint that returns a constant, or one that tests a dependency every server shares.
  • The single load balancer (ch. 3, Two of Everything): a diagram with two of every server and one box in front of them.
  • Autoscaling on the wrong signal (ch. 3, Two of Everything): a scaling rule on a metric the bottleneck does not move, such as memory on a service limited by CPU.
  • State on local disk (ch. 3, Two of Everything): an upload, a report or a session written to the server's own filesystem.

Data (chapters 4–8)

  • An index for every column (ch. 4, The Query That Read Every Row): a table with more indexes than queries, added "to be safe".
  • Offset pagination at depth (ch. 4, The Query That Read Every Row): OFFSET with a number supplied by the client.
  • N+1 queries (ch. 4, The Query That Read Every Row): a query inside a loop over the results of another query, often hidden by an object mapper.
  • The unbounded query (ch. 4, The Query That Read Every Row): a SELECT with no LIMIT on a table that grows.
  • Pool exhaustion (ch. 4, The Query That Read Every Row): requests failing with "timed out waiting for a connection" while the database's processors are not full.
  • Reading your own write from a replica (ch. 5, Copies of the Stock Book): a page shown immediately after a write whose query goes to a follower.
  • The failover never tested (ch. 5, Copies of the Stock Book): a failover described in a document and never carried out on purpose.
  • Asynchronous replication assumed durable (ch. 5, Copies of the Stock Book): a claim that "no committed data is lost" over a design with only asynchronous followers.
  • The replica as backup (ch. 5, Copies of the Stock Book): "we have replicas" given as the answer to "what if someone deletes the table?".
  • Check-then-act (ch. 6, Two Clerks, One Shelf): a read, an if in application code, then a write that depends on the read.
  • Assuming the default isolation level is serializable (ch. 6, Two Clerks, One Shelf): a design that says "it's in a transaction, so it's safe" and names no level.
  • The long transaction (ch. 6, Two Clerks, One Shelf): a network call, a file upload or user thinking time between BEGIN and COMMIT.
  • Inconsistent lock order (ch. 6, Two Clerks, One Shelf): two code paths that lock the same rows in different orders.
  • Sharding too early (ch. 7, Too Big for One Depot): a partitioning design with no figure for the write rate or data size one machine could not take.
  • The monotonic partition key (ch. 7, Too Big for One Depot): range partitioning on a timestamp or a counter in order to spread writes.
  • The hot partition (ch. 7, Too Big for One Depot): one partition at full utilisation while the others are quiet.
  • Hash modulo N (ch. 7, Too Big for One Depot): hash(key) % numberOfNodes in routing code.
  • Routine cross-partition transactions (ch. 7, Too Big for One Depot): an everyday operation that must change rows in two partitions atomically.
  • A database chosen by fashion (ch. 8, A Shelf for Every Kind of Thing): a store selected before anyone has listed the queries or the write rate.
  • Polyglot sprawl (ch. 8, A Shelf for Every Kind of Thing): a new kind of store with each new feature and no owner for its backups.
  • The search index as source of truth (ch. 8, A Shelf for Every Kind of Thing): a write that goes to the search index first, or data that exists nowhere else.
  • Blobs in the database (ch. 8, A Shelf for Every Kind of Thing): a column of images or documents in a transactional table.
  • Schemaless meaning no schema (ch. 8, A Shelf for Every Kind of Thing): "we don't need migrations" beside reading code full of checks for missing fields.

Speed (chapters 9–12)

  • The cache as source of truth (ch. 9, The Shelf by the Counter): data written to the cache and nowhere else, or a decision such as a charge made from a cached value.
  • No expiry (ch. 9, The Shelf by the Counter): a put without a time to live.
  • Stampede on expiry (ch. 9, The Shelf by the Counter): a database load graph with regular spikes at the cache's time to live.
  • Caching to hide a slow query (ch. 9, The Shelf by the Counter): a cache added because one query takes seconds.
  • A personalised response under a shared key (ch. 9, The Shelf by the Counter): a cache key that names the page but not the customer, for a value that includes something about the customer.
  • The cold cache at deploy (ch. 9, The Shelf by the Counter): a cache held in each server's memory, or flushed on release.
  • Uncacheable by default (ch. 10, Closer to the Customer): no-store, or no caching header at all, on files that are identical for every visitor.
  • Purging instead of versioning (ch. 10, Closer to the Customer): a release step that calls the network's purge function for files whose names did not change.
  • Private pages cached at the edge (ch. 10, Closer to the Customer): public, or a missing private, on a response that contains one customer's data.
  • The long DNS time to live before a move (ch. 10, Closer to the Customer): a record with a lifetime of a day on a name that is about to change address.
  • The unprotected origin (ch. 10, Closer to the Customer): an origin address that answers requests from anywhere.
  • The unbounded queue (ch. 11, The Yard Was Full): a queue with no maximum length and a producer that has never had a publish refused.
  • The queue as database (ch. 11, The Yard Was Full): code that inspects the queue to answer a question, or messages kept for days as the only record of something.
  • The invisible slow consumer (ch. 11, The Yard Was Full): monitoring of the broker's processor and disk with no alarm on depth or on the age of the oldest message.
  • Work that cannot be repeated (ch. 11, The Yard Was Full): a consumer that charges, prints or sends with no way to recognise a message it has seen before.
  • Polling everything (ch. 12, Three Left): a timer in the page that requests a value every second from the origin.
  • Exactly-once assumed (ch. 12, Three Left): a consumer that adds, increments or sends for each record, with its bookmark saved in a separate step.
  • The fan-out storm (ch. 12, Three Left): one event producing a message per follower or viewer, with no limit on either.
  • A stream where a batch would do (ch. 12, Three Left): a streaming pipeline feeding a report read once a day.

Agreement (chapters 13–15)

  • "We chose CA" (ch. 13, Which Copy Is Right?): a design for several machines that claims consistency and availability and says partitions will not happen.
  • One consistency level for everything (ch. 13, Which Copy Is Right?): a single setting, strong or eventual, applied to every table.
  • Eventual consistency with no convergence story (ch. 13, Which Copy Is Right?): "it will be consistent eventually" with no statement of what reconciles diverged copies.
  • Silent last write wins (ch. 13, Which Copy Is Right?): conflict resolution by timestamp on whole records, with nothing logged.
  • Home-made consensus (ch. 14, Two Head Offices): leader election written in application code, with a table of heartbeats and a "who is alive" query.
  • A lock without a fencing token (ch. 14, Two Head Offices): a distributed lock with an expiry, and writes that carry nothing the store can check.
  • A timeout taken as proof of death (ch. 14, Two Head Offices): a failover that acts on silence and does nothing to stop the old leader.
  • The two-node cluster (ch. 14, Two Head Offices): two voters, or two sites with no third.
  • Ordering by wall clock (ch. 15, What Time Is It?): a comparison of timestamps that were taken on different machines, in a sort, a merge or a conflict rule.
  • The auto-increment identifier across partitions (ch. 15, What Time Is It?): a database sequence used as the key of data that is, or will be, written in more than one place.
  • A timestamp as a unique identifier (ch. 15, What Time Is It?): a key built from the time to the millisecond.
  • Trusting the client's clock (ch. 15, What Time Is It?): a time sent by a browser or a phone and used to order, expire or validate.

Staying up (chapters 16–20)

  • The per-server rate limit (ch. 16, The Doorman): a limit held in each server's memory behind a load balancer.
  • Retries without jitter (ch. 16, The Doorman): a retry delay that is a constant or a pure power of two.
  • Limiting after the expensive work (ch. 16, The Doorman): a limiter that runs after authentication, parsing or a database read.
  • Shedding without priorities (ch. 16, The Doorman): an overload policy that drops requests at random, or oldest first, whatever they are.
  • Hedging a request that is not idempotent (ch. 16, The Doorman): a duplicate request sent for speed on a call that creates or charges.
  • Backups never restored (ch. 17, The Day the Region Went Dark): a backup job with a green tick and no record of a restore.
  • Failover never practised (ch. 17, The Day the Region Went Dark): a recovery document older than the last change to the system.
  • Active-active without a conflict design (ch. 17, The Day the Region Went Dark): two regions accepting writes to the same records, and "the database replicates both ways" as the whole answer.
  • The shared dependency across zones (ch. 17, The Day the Region Went Dark): one service, in one zone, that every zone calls: configuration, sessions, a registry.
  • A recovery plan that needs the failed region (ch. 17, The Day the Region Went Dark): a recovery step that fetches something, an image, a secret or the plan itself, from the place being recovered from.
  • An objective of one hundred percent (ch. 18, Promises with Numbers): "zero downtime" as a target, or four nines chosen because it sounds right.
  • An alert for every cause (ch. 18, Promises with Numbers): a pager that fires on processor, memory and disk thresholds.
  • An agreement without an objective (ch. 18, Promises with Numbers): a contractual availability figure that engineering does not measure, or one stricter than the internal target.
  • Blame in the postmortem (ch. 18, Promises with Numbers): a root cause that is a person's name, or "human error".
  • No error-budget policy (ch. 18, Promises with Numbers): an objective on a dashboard and no agreed consequence for missing it.
  • Résumé-driven scaling (ch. 19, The Bill): a technology proposed with its famous users named and its required load unstated.
  • Scaling for load that never came (ch. 19, The Bill): a component sized from a forecast, running at a few percent busy a year later.
  • Ignoring egress (ch. 19, The Bill): a design that copies data between regions, or out to another company, with no figure for bytes a month.
  • Never scaling back (ch. 19, The Bill): a capacity increase with a start date and no end date.
  • Boxes before requirements (ch. 20, The Drop): a design presented as a diagram, with no sentence saying what must be true.
  • A design with no numbers (ch. 20, The Drop): "a large spike" or "high traffic" where a rate should be.
  • A single design with no alternative (ch. 20, The Drop): a proposal with no section on what else was considered.
  • Ignoring failure modes (ch. 20, The Drop): a diagram in which every arrow works.
  • Building for permanent peak (ch. 20, The Drop): capacity sized for the one extreme hour and left in place.

The numbers card

Orders of magnitude (chapter 2).

Operation Time If a memory read took one second
Read from memory 100 ns 1 second
Read from a solid-state disk 100 µs 17 minutes
Round trip inside one data centre 0.5 ms 83 minutes
Round trip between continents 150 ms 17 days

Waiting against utilisation (chapter 1): response = service time ÷ (1 − utilisation). At 50% busy a request takes twice its service time; at 80%, five times; at 90%, ten; at 99%, a hundred.

Availability Downtime in a year Downtime in 30 days

The design method card

  1. Requirements. What must always be true, and what may give.
  2. Estimates. A peak rate per second, with its multiplier; storage; bandwidth.
  3. Interface. The few operations, and what each returns when refused.
  4. Data model. The records, the one place each is written, and what is conditional.
  5. High-level design. Boxes, each justified by a line in step 2.
  6. Deep dives. The hot key, the slowest dependency, the largest fan-out.
  7. Failure modes. For each box, what customers see when it fails.
  8. Trade-offs. What was given up, what was not built, and the measurement that would change the decision.

The timeline

Three eras. In the first, the theory was written, mostly for machines that shared a room. In the second, a few very large websites outgrew the single database and published what they built in its place. In the third, the rest of the industry adopted those designs and then learned to ask whether it needed them.

To 1999: the foundations. Queueing, the relational model, transactions, the B-tree and the logical clock are all older than the web. So are the first answers to its growth: consistent hashing, the content delivery network and consensus.

2000 to 2010: the large websites. Brewer named the trade that Google and Amazon were about to make in public. Memcached, MapReduce, Bigtable, Dynamo and Chubby each replaced something a single machine used to do, and by 2010 the costs of the trade had names too.

2011 onward: everyone else, and second thoughts. The log, understandable consensus and trustworthy clocks made the large designs available to ordinary teams. Then came the practices for running them, and the essays asking whether a given team should.
